utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, will you please call the cases.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-10-A, the Prosecutor versus Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, do I take it that it is understood that under that rubric there are really two appeals, one by the Prosecutor against acquittal and the other by Mr. Jelisic against sentence? Now, if that is understood, I would ask for appearances at this time. I take it the same counsel would be appearing for the same party in both appeals. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Then the first appeal, chronologically speaking, is the appeal by the Prosecution. So could I hear from the Prosecution what counsel would be appearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, I'm Upawansa Yapa, appearing for the Prosecution, with Mr. Geoffrey Nice, Morten Bergsmo, Fabricio Guariglia, and Ms. Carmela Annink-Javier is the case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And you will be appearing for the Prosecution in both appeals.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And for Mr. Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I'm William Clegg, and I appear with Mr. Jovan Babic and Ms. Laura McQuitty for the defendant in both appeals. Could I just mention one caveat to what Your Honour said about a moment ago about whether the appeal on behalf of the defendant was confined merely to sentence. Until yesterday, it was certainly confined merely to sentence. Yesterday, when I arrived in The Hague, I was given a copy of the Celebici judgement from the Appeals Chamber. The judgement that I anticipate His Honour Judge Nieto-Navia and His Honour Judge Pocar will be much more familiar with than I, but on reading the relevant passages, it seems that the principle of cumulative convictions would apply to the pleas tendered by this defendant to this indictment. The point is, in many senses, a totally academic point of no practical effect on the outcome of this case because he received one single penalty, a penalty I am confident that was imposed for his actions and not the way the indictment actually described the offences. However, in the Celebici case, although there was no double sentencing, only, in effect, cumulative convictions, the Appeals Chamber did refer the matter back to a Trial Chamber because in its view the sentencing outcome, and I quote from paragraph 431 of the judgement, "May have been different." I do not assert in this case that the sentencing outcome would have been different, and the last thing that Mr. Jelisic would want would be for his appeal to be postponed as a result of this quite technical point. It does, however, seem to me that on the basis of the majority decision in the Celebici case, that the cumulative convictions returned against this defendant on the basis of his plea of guilty can't technically stand, and we would invite the Appeal Chamber to formally quash the lesser of each of the pair of offences for which he was sentenced. To my mind, this makes no practical effect on the outcome of the appeal at all, and I do not suggest that the penalty passed by the Trial Chamber would in any way have been different. But in the light of the Celebici judgement as I understand it, I don't think it would be right for me as counsel for Mr. Jelisic to, as it were, abandon a point that has found favour with the Appeal Chamber of this Court. Therefore, I would respectfully ask for leave from the Court to appeal against the lesser of each of the pairs of offences that Jelisic pleaded guilty to. I would invite the Court to quash those convictions on the basis of the judgement in the Celebici case and then to proceed to hear the appeal on its merits so far as the appeal of the Prosecution is concerned against the acquittal of genocide, and so far as the defendant is concerned, on the issue of his sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Court has before it a motion to amend the Notice of Appeal in one of the two cases. What does the Prosecution say?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour, we are not taken by surprise by my learned friend's submission because this morning at about 9.00 he informed me that he proposed to take up this issue. But as it is, Your Honour, what I would wish to submit is, although my learned friend puts it simply as a matter of academic interest, this is not a matter on which we can commit ourselves by responding on our feet, and it may require us to look into the implications of the Celebici judgement on the, on the judgement before Your Honours at this moment. So I have no objection to my learned friend raising the issue or making submissions on the matter, but may I be permitted to request that we be permitted to file written submissions, if it is required, in respect of this question on a later occasion. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, you would like a word in addition?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: If the rules permitted, I would merely observe that Mr. Yapa was, of course, the lead counsel for the Prosecutor in the Celebici appeal so I anticipate knows a great deal more about it than I, and I would have thought he would have been able to deal with the fairly simple proposition that I make in the light of his appearance in the appeal personally without the need to descend to lengthy written submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, the position is that there are some members of the bench who may not be as familiar as you and Mr. Yapa happen to be with the judgement to which you are referring, so may there be some merit in Mr. Yapa's proposal that, if only to educate the members of the bench, it would be a good idea if the parties were allowed in due course to file written papers on the point. That is to say, briefly, as I understand it, the Prosecution offers no objection to your proposal to amend your Notice of Appeal, and appeals can go on, the hearing can go on on that basis; but I imagine that at a subsequent stage, the parties would be granted leave -- or we will grant leave now to the parties to file at a subsequent stage written briefs on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I'm very content for the matter to proceed in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, then, leave is granted on those conditions. We will stipulate later what might be the time frame for submissions for the written briefs and if any party so desires. And second item is, housekeeping -- have you finished with that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I have. I had forgot to mention that I do have the assistance of an interpreter, that Mr. Babic's English is much better than my Serbo-Croat, but I'm afraid communication between the two of us is still a struggle. She is present outside Court, can only enter with the leave of the Court, and I would ask for leave for her to enter Court to sit between the two of us and also to enable me to communicate directly with Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us hear from your friend. Mr. Prosecutor, is there any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Agreed. Very good. May I go on to some housekeeping details. We began to sit this morning at 9.30, and we propose to continue on until 1.00 p.m. Now, the luncheon break will follow and normally that will be an hour and a half, but we propose to resume at 3.00, the reason being that one of our number would have to take his place on another Bench during the interval. So we would resume at 3.00, and we would continue on until 5.00 to 5.15 p.m. today. There will be, in the usual way, two coffee breaks, about 15 minutes each. Now, we will begin with the Prosecutor's appeal, and as we have indicated in a Scheduling Order, each main presenter will have two hours to present his case, and the party following would then have two hours to respond and then the first speaker will have half an hour to wrap it up, as it were. We will take the Prosecutor's appeal first, and when that will have been concluded, we will follow with Mr. Jelisic's appeal. Now, we did, in one of our Scheduling Orders, ask the parties to be good enough to file public versions of certain documents. I think the Prosecutor complied. They filed a respondent's brief on the 6th of September, but on our records, we don't see that any briefs -- any public versions of any briefs were filed by the Defence. I wonder if this might be remedied as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It certainly will be done as soon as possible. As the Appeals Chamber may be aware, I was only instructed inside the last three weeks and was unaware of that Scheduling Order, but I will ensure that it is complied with in the immediate future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We appreciate fully, Mr. Clegg, the disadvantages under which you suffer, and we also admire your ability to conform. So what we propose is that we shall go on with the appeal pending the submission of these public versions of the various documents by the Defence. Now, there is a skeleton argument presented by Mr. Clegg, and the Bench understands the Prosecution's position to be this: The Prosecution thinks that there may be some new arguments in the skeleton brief, but that the Prosecution is offering no objection to its being filed. Mr. Clegg, you were asking for it to be laid over formally?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I am. It was not intended to raise any new argument, but I see that it has been interpreted as so doing. I was hoping to effectively clear the decks and to clarify the points that will still be pursued by the appellant and those that would not be, but I have no objection to the respondent, or should I say appellant, as it were, embracing the fresh material in the course of their arguments today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You propose to stay within the perimeter demarcated by the previous pleadings filed on behalf of Mr. Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes, as I understand them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, also in the skeleton arguments presented by Mr. Clegg there is an announcement of certain concessions. Those, I take it, will be taken into account. If they could lead to an abbreviation or curtailment of our comment, that is a prospect much to be desired. The last thing is the parties will bear in mind and alert the Bench when the occasion arises to the possible need for a closed session on any particular phase of the arguments. Right. So we'll hear the Prosecution at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, before I commence on the Prosecution case or the Prosecution case in appeal, may I be permitted to hand over a short document that I have prepared in respect of the order of argument of the Prosecution, which I'm sure will assist Your Honours and also my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Yapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honours. One other small matter that I wish to refer to -- Your Honours were pleased to give -- allocate the times for the presentation of arguments, and we have been given two hours for the presentation of the appeal and another two hours for the response. On consideration, we have agreed that it may not be necessary for us to have the two hours that have been demarcated for the response, and may Your Honours be pleased to allocate half an hour from that response time to the appeal time, for the presentation of appeal, to make it two and a half hours, and then one and a half hours for the response. There is no difference in the time allocation for the Prosecution, but the request is that we be given an additional half an hour taken from the response time to present the appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, you don't offer an objection to the course proposed, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I have no objection. It appears as though the initial hopes of brevity may have been rather premature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I say, Mr. Yapa, that the Bench has read the briefs which have been submitted. There is documentation of some dimensions before the Court, and we had hoped that in this way it would be possible for arguments to be abbreviated a little. Still, provided you do not exceed the maximum times allocated on the Scheduling Order, we would be disposed to allow you to take the course which you have indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour. I fully appreciate the observations made by Your Honour on the written brief that I will file. We have made -- I have made attempts to make it as comprehensive as possible, and we have done so. The order of submissions that will be made will be in addition to any matter that has to be elaborated on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You're aware, Mr. Yapa, that the rule-making body has since issued a practice direction regulating the maximum length of written briefs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, yes. May it please Your Honours, my task at this stage is, as indicated in the order of argument, to present an introduction to the Prosecution appeal and later speak on the remedies sought by the Prosecution in the appeal. The second aspect that is in respect of the remedies, it may be necessary for another counsel in my team to make submissions, but that will be decided upon later on. Your Honour, as regards the grounds of appeal taken up by the Prosecution, what I would wish to at the very outset state to Your Honours 1 is that we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Yapa, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: My colleague on my left has pointed out that you have started roughly at 10.00, and that should be borne in mind as a factor in the computation of allocated times. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honours. The submission that I wish to make initially is following upon the pronouncement made by Your Honours' Court that the appeal procedure in this Tribunal is of a corrective nature, in terms of the Statute, the Prosecution has come before Your Honours seeking relief under Article 25 of the Statute. In the appeals that have come up so far before Your Honours' Court, the Prosecution has made submissions on the standards of review on appeal. I do not intend to reiterate those submissions other than to say that we are before Your Honours as an appealing party, taking grounds of appeal brought on issues of law and facts. This appeal, although it is from a final judgement of a Trial Chamber, has different features from appeals heard by Your Honours' Court so far. It is an appeal from a final judgement pronounced not at the conclusion of a trial as we ordinarily refer to; the appeal is against a judgement at a previous stage of the trial. The stage that I referred to is described as a halfway stage by some judges. The stage I am drawing attention to is Rule 98 bis stage as is commonly referred to now in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The grounds of appeal that the Prosecution has taken up are germane to the operation of this rule. It is in fact the central theme of the appeal of the Prosecution. Arguments in this regard are to be followed, but may I submit it -- may I submit that it is our submission that an inaccurate and erroneous procedure was followed by the Trial Chamber. Proceeding on that submission is our first ground of appeal -- as our first ground of appeal, we submit that the Trial Chamber erred in law by depriving the Prosecution an opportunity to be heard prior to the Trial Chamber proceeding to act under Rule 98 bis. There are two facets to the first ground of appeal that we have urged. The Prosecution was denied a right to be heard on the application of Rule 98 bis. Concomitantly, the Trial Chamber refused the Prosecution the right to be heard on the question whether the Prosecution should be granted a hearing. It is not my task to go into detail on the grounds of appeal that we have taken up. Suffice it to say that flowing from the error of denying the Prosecution the right to be heard, the Trial Chamber erred in law in the application of Rule 98 bis, and further, erred in law in defining the requisite mental state for genocide under Article 4 of the Statute. In a sense, then, we have taken up three grounds of appeal. The first is on the Prosecution's right to be heard; the second centres on the application of Rule 98 bis, more particularly, in construing the rule, the application of a beyond-reasonable-doubt standard; and the third is on the mental state for genocide in Article 4 of the Statute. These grounds of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. appeal will be elaborated on by my colleagues shortly. May I be permitted to make a general submission in respect of all three grounds of appeal. These grounds of appeal deal with issues crucial and fundamental to proceedings before the Trial Chamber. The grounds are interrelated and interconnected, so much so it could be said that there was a chain reaction from the initial error. Before I speak of the remedy we are seeking, I would like to say a few words about the skeleton submissions presented by the appellant. We are not opposed to the presentation. We are, in fact, thankful to my learned friend for presenting the skeleton argument. As regards the appeal of the Defence, it is stated that the appellant seeks only to appeal against his sentence. Significantly, the appellant concedes the first two grounds of appeal of the Prosecution, going to the extent of saying that for the reasons advanced by the Prosecution, the Prosecution ought to have been given the opportunity to be heard; and for the reasons submitted by the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber did apply the incorrect standard of proof to the stage at which the trial had reached. I'm quoting my learned friend's submission in the skeleton argument. The appellant maintains the position that the Trial Chamber correctly applied the law of genocide to the facts of the case. We take issue on this assertion and necessary submissions will be made when presenting the arguments on the third ground of appeal of the Prosecution. In conceding the first two grounds of appeal, the appellant adds a rider, as if it were. On the first ground of appeal, it is said that the failure to permit the Prosecution an opportunity to make submissions does not render the verdict invalid unless the Trial Chamber erred in its application of the law to the facts of the case. It is submitted that with respect. It is submitted with respect that this is a misconceived submission. Necessary submissions will be made on this aspect when dealing with the first ground of appeal. On the second ground, the appellant having conceded that the complaint was well-founded adds that it relates to form rather than substance. We beg to disagree. It is not one of mere form. It was a serious error which scuttled the settled procedure and led to a series of errors of law and fact. Our submission on this ground will deal with this matter later. The submission that the Trial Chamber short-circuited - again, I'm quoting the skeleton argument - the proper process is, with respect, not an acceptable submission because there is no room for such a procedure. If I may come to the remedies that we are seeking, in short, may I say to Your Honours, submit to Your Honours, that in essence, we are seeking a retrial on the count of genocide before a differently constituted Trial Chamber. Detailed submissions on this matter will be made by my colleagues in the appeals team. We also urge Your Honours to give guidance on the legal issue of the necessary intent in the crime of genocide. I do not wish to proceed any further. On the first ground of appeal, it will be Mr. Fabricio Guariglia who will make the submissions. I seek your permission to invite Mr. Guariglia to make his submissions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Guariglia, you have the floor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, I would deal with grounds one and two of the Prosecution's appeal brief, hopefully in no longer than 20 minutes, subject to questions. As already advanced, the concessions made by the Defence are welcomed, and we see them as confirming our position that the Trial Chamber erred. However, the fact that the parties agree on a particular point of law does not automatically dispose of the issue, and we submit that the Appeals Chamber must still be satisfied that the points agreed by the parties constitute correct determinations of the law and is free to move beyond the submissions of the parties if it considers that the position adopted by the parties is legally incorrect. Further in this case, as already explained by Mr. Yapa, there is no complete agreement between the parties as to the scope of those errors and the effect of those errors under grounds 1 and 2 of the Prosecution's appeal brief generate or trigger. I will first address the issues on the Prosecution's first ground of appeal as contained in paragraphs 2.1 to 2.40 of the Prosecution's appeal brief and explain why in and of itself the Trial Chamber's refusal to hear submissions of the Prosecution before entering a judgement of acquittal warrants a retrial. The overarching principle here is that also the Prosecution is entitled to a fair and expeditious trial under Article 20, paragraph 1 of the statute. We rely on the clear findings of this Appeals Chamber in a decision delivered in the Aleksovski case pursuant to an interlocutory appeal. The concept of a fair trial must be applied in favour of both parties since the Prosecution acts on behalf of and in the interest of the International Community, including the interest of the victims of the crimes charged. Therefore, a trial could not be considered to be fair where the Prosecution is favoured at the expense of the Prosecution's rights. The right to be heard before a decision that may be a final decision on a case is made, as it will always be the case in the context of a Rule 98 bis determination, is a fundamental right of either party that goes to the core of fairness of criminal proceedings. It constitutes an essential component of adversarial proceedings which rely on the premise that partisan advocacy on both sides is the means to promote the ultimate goal that the guilty be convicted and the innocent go free. It is recognised as an absolute right by the ICTY Rules themselves, contrary to the position adopted by the Trial Chamber in its oral judgement in the Jelisic case. Rule 86 grants both parties an absolute right to make closing submissions before a final decision on the case is reached. Conversely, the Rule does not grant any authority to a Trial Chamber to refuse to hear closing arguments by the parties. A fortiori, being a decision to enter a judgement of acquittal under Rule 98 bis a final decision on the case, we submit, an identical right of audience should be granted to the parties before the decision is reached. We submit that the right of the Prosecution to be heard in the context of Rule 98 bis cannot and should not be reduced to a hollow right which may be freely ignored or reduced to a meaningless minimum by a Trial Chamber without fatally impairing the integrity of the proceedings as the Defence is now inviting you to do. On the contrary; we submit that the right is of such a fundamental nature that it is impossible to see how a trial could still be considered to be fair within the meaning of Article 20, paragraph 1 when the right in question has been completely violated by an absolute denial of a Trial Chamber to hear arguments before making a decision. In this context, it will be pertinent to identify with some precision the events at trial pertaining to this ground of appeal. The situation that you must examine is not one in which the Prosecution inadvertently failed to use an available opportunity to address the Trial Chamber, thereby arguably waiving its right to be heard, nor is the situation one in which the Prosecution's prejudice was caused by a Trial Chamber's excessive limitation of the exercise of the right to be heard. In either of these hypothetical cases, the argument of a harmless error could perhaps be validly raised, but in the instant case, the Prosecution had no opportunity whatsoever to present arguments to the Trial Chamber pertaining to the Rule 98 bis decision. When the Prosecution requested the Trial Chamber precisely to grant it that very opportunity, it met an outright refusal of the Trial Chamber to hear arguments. The final decision on the case, an acquittal, immediately followed that refusal. In addition to these considerations, it may also be pertinent to bear in mind the importance for Chambers of the International Tribunal of hearing submissions by the parties in order properly determine the issues at stake. In the context of the adversarial proceedings adopted by the ICTY, submissions by both parties provide Chambers of the Tribunal with the very material that they need in order to make sound and reasoned decision on both law and fact. Regardless of whether it is acting upon request of a party or proprio motu, a Trial Chamber needs to hear submissions from parties before making a decision in order to have the opportunity to consider all aspects of the case before it. The damaging consequences of not hearing submissions from the parties before making a central decision on the case and conversely the benefits of being assisted by the parties are perhaps most clearly represented by the Trial Chamber's adoption of a defective standard for the evaluation of the evidence under Rule 98 bis in the instant case. By refusing to hear arguments from the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber deprived itself of the benefit of being assisted as to what the proper standard under Rule 98 bis would be. As a result, we submit, the Trial Chamber completely erred on the matter by inadequately adopting a test of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, and the conclusive language of both the oral and written judgements clearly shows that the Trial Chamber did not even consider as a possibility that a different test could apply for that particular exercise. In contrast, two Judges of the same Trial Chamber, when faced in a different case with a motion of acquittal under Rule 98 bis, the case being Prosecutor versus Kvocka, and after hearing detailed submissions by all parties, instead of insisting in applying the test that they had previously applied in the Jelisic case, adopted a test identical to the one advocated by the Prosecution in the current appellate proceedings. It may well be concluded that those Judges, in light of the submissions they had heard, realised that their previous decision on the matter had been in error. Perhaps the Jelisic Trial Chamber would have realised that it was about to apply the wrong test had it decided to hear arguments from the Prosecution. To sum up on ground 1, the right to be heard before a final decision on a case is made is a fundamental one, and it constitutes an essential component of the fairness of trial proceedings. Its violation by a Trial Chamber constitutes such a fundamental blow to the fairness of a trial, as required by Article 20, paragraph 1, that in and of itself it renders the decision invalid and warrants a retrial. This is much more so where the violation, as in the instant case, is compounded by an absolute denial of the right to be heard. Further, depriving a party from an opportunity to be heard not only violates that party's fundamental rights, but also puts at risk the integrity and quality of the proceedings by undermining the cornerstone of the very system of judicial decision-making in an adversarial setting, partisan advocacy from both sides. We respectfully submit that, contrary to the assertions of my learned friend, there is no need for the Appeals Chamber to make any further determination as to the impact of the alleged error on the decision. On the basis of the error invoked in ground 1 alone, we submit, a retrial before a reconstituted Trial Chamber should be ordered. However, if the Appeals Chamber considers that a further showing of impact on the decision is required, we submit that in the instant case there can be no doubt that the Trial Chamber's failure to hear submissions by the Prosecution did cause fundamental defects in the decision such as adoption of an effective standard under Rule 98 bis, which will be discussed under ground 2, the numerous fundamental errors of the Trial Chamber in its evaluation of the evidence before it, and the application of the law on genocide which will be discussed under ground 3. This concludes my submission on ground 1. Unless there are questions from the Chamber, I will move to ground 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Guariglia, members of the Bench would be asking you questions whenever they feel disposed to, but let me take the precaution of asking whether they intend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No. You may go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Similar conclusions to the ones reached in ground 1 may be properly reached also on the issues pertaining to the Prosecution's second ground of appeal, that is, the application of a guilt beyond a reasonable doubt standard under Rule 98 bis. As already said, the Defence, while conceding that the Trial Chamber erred in applying the standard is inviting you to treat this error as one of form rather than substance. It would appear that the Defence position is that since the Trial Chamber operates both as a trier of fact and a trier of law, the fact that the Chamber advanced its ultimate determination on guilt or innocence to the Rule 98 bis stage is immaterial since the Trial Chamber would have acquitted at the end of the case in any event. By arguing this way, the Defence is suggesting that the success of the Prosecutor's second ground of appeal necessarily depends on the success of the Prosecutor's third ground of appeal dealing with the quality and volume of the evidence and the law on genocide. The Prosecution respectfully disagrees. At the outset, the Prosecution notes that the Defence has attempted first to isolate the errors committed by the Trial Chamber and then taking each error individually, to undermine their importance. That this exercise must fail necessarily in the case of the violation of the Prosecution's right to be heard has already been explained. In addition, the Prosecution submits that on the one hand, there are very compelling reasons to consider that a complete failure to apply the correct test under Rule 98 bis should be treated as an incurable error that goes beyond the corrective ability of the Appeals Chamber. On the other hand, the Prosecution submits that the errors committed by the Trial Chamber are intimately interrelated and must be considered as a totality. I will address these questions in the remaining time. It appears to be beyond dispute that because of the reasons advanced in paragraphs 3.1 to 3.58 of the Prosecution's appeal brief the Trial Chamber erred when applying the test of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt in the context of Rule 98 bis, and it must be noted that of the eight decisions to date dealing with motions of acquittal before the International Tribunal, the Jelisic one is the only decision to advance a test of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt to a halfway stage of the proceedings. If the position is accepted that the Trial Chamber erred by acting in that way, then the question before you is whether you should on that basis alone remand the case for a new trial, or whether you still need to take a further step and determine whether the error renders the decision unsafe as advocated by my learned friend. Our position, as I already said, is twofold: We submit that the Appeals Chamber may properly conclude that the Trial Chamber's error goes beyond the corrective ability of the Appeals Chamber and simply cannot be cured by recourse to a theory of no substantial wrong or any other equivalent construction. In the instant case, proceedings were prematurely mutilated by a wrongful decision under Rule 98 bis. The Appeals Chamber may consider that it would be inappropriate to engage in an exercise of speculation as to how the case may have evolved had the Trial Chamber applied the correct standard and decided that there was a case to answer. Instead, the Appeals Chamber may wish to apply a purely objective test to the real issue before it, not whether this Trial Chamber would have acquitted the accused, but whether there was evidence on which a reasonable Trial Chamber could have convicted the accused. If the answer to that question is an affirmative one, the Appeals Chamber may validly conclude that the Prosecution was entitled to have its case answered by the Defence and determined by the Trial Chamber acting as a trier of fact. On that basis alone, the Appeals Chamber could, and we would respectfully submit should, order a retrial. Needless to say if the conclusion reached by the Appeals Chamber is that there was no evidence upon which a reasonable Trial Chamber could convict, then the Trial Chamber's error would be reduced to an unfortunate but harmless election of words. That this is not the case is demonstrated by the Trial Chamber's assessment of the evidence, and its weighing of the evidence, and will be clarified by my colleague Geoffrey Nice when dealing with the Prosecution's third ground of appeal. The Prosecution submits that by ordering a retrial without having to evaluate the correctness or substantive justice of the judgement, the Appeals Chamber would ensure at least three beneficial results for ICTY proceedings. First, it will preserve the Appeals Chamber from having to enter into an exercise of speculation as to what position the Defence could have taken; to further assess the evidentiary consequences of that speculative decision; and finally, to determine whether a conviction based on that purely hypothetical scenario would be unreasonable, a task that may be considered to be inappropriate for an appellate court. Second, it would ensure that final decisions on law and fact are subject to the proper two-stage process, first instance and appeal, instead of being reduced to a single stage of discussion as it is happening in the instant case. We consider it to be applicable to the instant case, the position adopted by Judge Shahabuddeen's in an interlocutory appeal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. delivered in the ICTR case Kanyabashi versus the Prosecutor. The Appeals Chamber should not be deciding the issues that have not been discussed before a Trial Chamber therefore without having the assistance and benefit of that Trial Chamber from the decision of which the appeal is sought to be brought. This is particularly important in the case at bar where matters pertaining to the volume and quality of the evidence and the applicable law were simply never discussed before a Trial Chamber. The third benefit of adopting the suggested process is that it would ensure uniform application of Rule 98 bis and discourage Trial Chambers from mingling their functions as triers of law and triers of fact, a very dangerous exercise that has in the instant case caused prejudice to the Prosecution, but that can be fatal to the rights of the Defence if a Trial Chamber considers that it is free to decide whether guilt beyond a reasonable doubt is established and decides in a particular case that it has been established under Rule 98 bis. We accordingly submit that the error of the Trial Chamber must be considered to be a fatal one that cannot be cured by the Appeals Chamber through recourse to auxiliary methods of analysis such as no substantial wrong doctrine, and that, per se, it justifies a retrial. At the same time and as already advanced, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber's failure to give the Prosecution an opportunity to be heard coupled with this flawed determination of the applicable standard under Rule 98 bis must be seen as components of a single process of a improper judicial adjudication. By acting the way it did, the Trial Chamber did not only cause irreparable damage in the integrity of the proceedings but also to the quality and reliability of its product. We submit that the quality of a Trial Chamber's decision in a given case relies on the quality of its procedure. In the instant case, the cumulative effect of errors of such a fundamental nature infects the whole process to such an extent that the decision reached simply can no longer be trusted. There is no need to make a determination as to whether the judgement is correct. If it was, and we respectfully submit it is not; it would only be a matter of chance. Simultaneously, this accumulation of fundamental errors impacts so intensively on the integrity and image of the proceedings that both process and decision fail to meet the basic requirement of Lord Hewitt's maxim as recalled by this Appeals Chamber in the Furundzija case. In the instant case, justice was not seen to be done. To conclude, the Prosecution considers that there is no merit in the respondent's contention that the Trial Chamber's failure to apply the correct standard under Rule 98 bis is merely an error of form incapable in and of itself of rendering the decision invalid. For the reasons that have been advanced, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber's error could and should not be condoned ex post facto, as the respondent is now inviting you to do, and that accordingly, a new trial should be ordered. Your Honours, this concludes my submissions on both grounds one and two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One question by Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Guariglia, as far as the standard, your ground 2, as far as the standard that a Trial Chamber should use in ruling under 98 bis on a motion for judgement of acquittal, most of the authorities, apart from those inside the Tribunal, that you have cited to us which adopt the standard which you are proposing to us, namely, that no reasonable Chamber could find that there was not reasonable doubt, most of those decisions deal with the situation where the judge is making the ruling on acquittal but ultimately a jury, a different fact finder, must make the ultimate decision on whether there is reasonable doubt. So it's easy, at least for me, to see why you would not let the judge take over the ultimate jury function subjectively. But why would that same standard apply in a situation where you will have exactly the same fact finders at the end of the trial as at the time of acquittal, and the Prosecution must, as you concede, bear the burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Well, it's a very important question, Your Honour. At the outset, it is true the test is usually adopted by common law jurisdictions and in the context of jury trials. However, in a number of common law jurisdictions, as in the case of the UK when dealing with summary proceedings, even in criminal proceedings before a single judge operating both as trier of fact and trier of law, the standard remains the same. And we would submit that the standard remains the same in order to ensure basic principles of predictability and legal certainty in criminal proceedings. The moment standards are getting interchangeable, criminal proceedings start getting unpredictable. If a Trial Chamber has the authority to decide to advance a determination of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt to the Rule 98 bis stage, then that operates both ways. It will eventually operate against an accused. If the Trial Chamber is authorised to embark into that kind of analysis, a Trial Chamber is then free to determine halfway through the proceedings that guilt beyond a reasonable doubt has been established. That will create automatically a burden on the accused to disprove that premature finding of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, to persuade the Trial Chamber that, contrary to its finding, the accused is innocent. Now, this would be contrary to the Statute of this institution under which an accused does not have such a burden. But the problem is that if there is no certainty as to what standard would be applied in the context of Rule 98 bis, we engage in a vicious circle because the burden of persuasion that the Prosecution, for instance, will ordinarily use in the context of a Rule 98 bis scenario is much lower than the burden of persuasion that you will use at the end of the case during closing arguments where the Prosecution will marshal both evidence and law for the purpose of persuading a Trial Chamber that guilt beyond a reasonable doubt has been established. If the standard under Rule 98 bis is ambiguous, we also get into this vicious circle in which, sooner or later, an accused will be found guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the middle of trial proceedings and not where it should properly be found, if appropriate, upon completion of trial proceedings after all evidence has been presented and closing arguments from both sides have been heard.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me try a question or two, Mr. Guariglia. Is my impression correct that you are taking an objection to the references by the Trial Chamber to a standard of proof of guilt beyond reasonable doubt when making a decision midway, as it were? Am I right in that impression?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: If I understood Your Honour's question correctly, yes, our objection is that the Trial Chamber advanced the ultimate test to a halfway determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. Is it reasonably possible to banish that notion altogether from the decision-making process at that stage? What I mean to put to you is this: There are various ways of putting the matter, mind you, but one way, traditional way, is to ask this question, whether the Prosecution's evidence, given at its highest, could support a guilty verdict by a jury properly directed. Now, if you focus on the words "properly directed," aren't we speaking there of a tribunal of fact being properly directed to this proposition, that you cannot find guilt except that it is proved beyond reasonable doubt? In other words, at this midway stage, is there a difference between making a present finding of guilt beyond reasonable doubt and saying that the Prosecution evidence, given at its highest, would not enable a tribunal of fact to find guilt on the basis of a standard of proof of guilt beyond reasonable doubt?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: The answer to Your Honour's question is, yes, there is a difference. It's a different intensity of the analysis of the evidence. And this is very clear in the context of the decisions that have been reached in this institution under Rule 98 bis where one can see the Trial Chamber's efforts not to affect themselves with a premature 5 in-depth evaluation of the evidence- the clearest example perhaps is that the Trial Chamber confines its analysis to determine whether there is material upon which the inference could be drawn at the end of the case of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt in matters pertaining to 7(1) criminal liability. But the Trial Chambers do not make that inference. They refrain from making that inference. They just say, "There is some material. On the basis of this material at end of the case we may, and then again, we may not, draw these inferences." So using language from the Kordic decision, Trial Chambers segregate their functions as triers of fact and triers of law. They preserve themselves for triers of fact for the final stages of the proceedings, and they analyse, if you want to put it this way, more superficially the evidence at that stage. And we think that is fundamental that this division be represerved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask a follow-up question like this: You have referred to the adversarial character of our proceedings. Would I be right in supposing - correct me if I'm wrong - that we must have regard to the difference between substance and form? Were the members of the Trial Chamber non-common law lawyers?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, now, is that a fact to be borne in mind this way: The substance of the law needs to be followed, but in reading what they said, should we bear in mind that the Trial Chamber in question was not a common law set of lawyers, so they may have used words which a common law lawyer would not normally use without intending to depart from the substance of the law. What do you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Well, at the outset, let me make clear, Your Honour, I'm a civil law lawyer myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Second part of your question, if I understand your question correctly, is whether the Trial Chamber simply applied the wrong label to the correct operation. And we would say no, it goes beyond that, and it transpires with clarity from the judgement, Your Honour. It is clear that the Trial Chamber knew what it was doing, knew what test it was going to apply and did intend to apply that test. And it did apply the test. It embarked on a detailed analysis of the evidence. It weighed the evidence. It looked at the inferences that it thought it could draw in that decision and thought it could not draw from that existent body of evidence. We respectfully submit that it wasn't that type of error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Guariglia, I'm indebted to you for your response, and I bear in mind that Mr. Clegg has conceded that not only did the Trial Chamber adopt the wrong standard, but it misapplied this standard to the facts. Is that correct, Mr. Clegg?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Our concession is that the words delivered by the Trial Chamber misstate the appropriate standard of proof at that stage of the trial, but we do not concede that they came to the wrong conclusion, nor had they expressed themselves differently would there have been no ground of appeal for the Prosecutor to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. What I have in mind -- thank you, Mr. Clegg, for that clarification. What I have in mind, Mr. Guariglia, is this: No doubt reading the oral judgement, I take it it's the oral judgement which is really pertinent to this matter, the judgement delivered on 19th of October. There are passages which support your thesis, and I do have regard to your very well-taken point that in the end, on matters of law it is the Court which has to decide, notwithstanding any agreement by the parties. Now, when you read that oral decision, maybe there are elements in it which could support the thesis which you are propounding, but let me read to you a passage or two and test you on these passages. Now, I have before me the transcript of the 19th of October, 1999, the English text, at page 2327. You have found it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The last paragraph on that page reads thus. The Presiding Judge is speaking. He says: "The Judges then reviewed all of the evidence put forth by the Prosecution. From their deliberations, they concluded that even without having to hear the possible arguments put forth by the Defence, the accused could not, could not be recognised as guilty of the crime of genocide." Were they, by the use of that language, to be understood as making a present judgement on guilt or innocence or were they to be understood as saying, "on this evidence, no reasonable tribunal of fact could bring in a verdict of guilty beyond a reasonable doubt"? Then at page 2332, they say this: They seem to make a distinction between the two categories of determination, that is, making a present finding of guilt and saying that on the evidence, no reasonable tribunal of fact could, in future, as it were, bring in a finding of guilt. At page 2332, second paragraph, they say: "Moreover, one must not confuse the notion of acquittal with that of a lack of evidence." That is, no Prosecution case. So they have in mind a distinction which is pertinent. They say this refers to a Prosecution argument which comes from another case which this Tribunal heard. That is the Blaskic case. Then they go on: "In the second case, it is sufficient for the Trial Chamber to consider that the Prosecutor has brought in enough proof for the Defence to be in -- to have a need to answer, that is, there was a case to answer." And if you look at the French text, in the French formulation it becomes clear that that was the test they were using, whether on the evidence presented by the Prosecution, if accepted, a reasonable tribunal of fact could, in future, bring in a verdict of guilty. Then at page 2337, you have this in the second full paragraph: "In the case in point, the Judges consider that the Prosecutor has not provided the sufficient proof which would allow us to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that Jelisic planned ..." et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. Now, bearing in mind that these were not common law Judges but non-common law Judges operating within an adversarial system and who, therefore, could not be expected to have the verbal orientation of normal common law Judges, how do you construe those three passages?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say in the light of those passages, the -- my basic conclusion would be that the Trial Chamber's fundamentation is very erratic in a number of ways and it is highly unclear. If I can draw your attention to the same passage where you're -- in paragraph -- on page 2338, 2337, I think, in your version of the transcript, when saying that: "The Prosecutor has not provided the sufficient proof that would allow us to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that accused Jelisic planned, incited, ordered," et cetera, the passage finishes by, "and this doubt must be found to the benefit of the accused," precisely what happens in the context of the determination of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt that is the clear distinction between a Rule 98 bis scenario where if you want to put it this way, the evidence is seen in the most favourable light to the Prosecution, whereas in the context 21 of a final determination of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, the doubt always goes in the benefit of the Accused, in dubio proreo. But further, Your Honour, we think that the oral judgement must be seen in conjunction with the written judgement, and in the written judgement you will find, at paragraph 15, that the Trial Chamber concludes that it was not possible to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that the choice of victims arose from the precise logic to destroy represented figures from the Muslim community. It says, paragraph 93: "It had also not been established beyond a reasonable doubt whether the accused killed at Luke camp under orders." Paragraph 95: "The Prosecution had not provided evidence that could establish beyond a reasonable doubt that there was a plan to destroy" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That could establish, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Allowing the Chamber to establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Guariglia, let me ask you a question like this: Is it correct to assume that even under the strict common law code, as it were, a Trial Judge is absolutely prevented from considering a question of doubt at this midway point? Is there perhaps a situation in which exceptionally he could say that the case for the Prosecution has completely broken down either through cross-examination or inconsistencies, et cetera? It's an exceptional situation, but in that exceptional situation, is he entitled to say, "Well, on this evidence, no reasonable tribunal of fact is likely to bring any verdict of guilty beyond a reasonable doubt," which standard will entitle the Trial Chamber in futuro to resolve questions of doubt? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely correct, but we do not see that as exceptions to a provision to apply an inference in favour of the accused or to advance somehow the test beyond a reasonable doubt. It's simply that the Prosecution case has broken down and there is no case to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 1 answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. Well, Mr. Guariglia, I wish you to understand me as merely putting to you questions for the benefit of your reaction and not as expressing any concluded opinion on the subject. I think that's normally understood by the bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: That's clearly understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I will leave then the floor to Mr. Morten Bergsmo, who will address you on the legal aspects of the Prosecution's third ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would it be the sense of the Bar that this would be an appropriate moment to take a break, in between speakers? Thank you. Well, 15 minutes then. We'll reassemble, let us say, at a quarter past the hour. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So now we will hear from Mr. Bergsmo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do forgive me if I don't pronounce the name correctly. You're going to speak on the third ground of appeal?

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to present three sets of observations on section 4(B) in the brief of appeal of the Prosecution, section 4(B); that is, I will address the requisite mental state under Article 4 of the Statute. My learned friend and colleague, Mr. Nice, will address the other subsections of section 4 in our brief after I have concluded my remarks. The three sets of observations I seek to present are, first, a clarification of what the submission of the Prosecution is in section 4(B); second, an explanation why the Prosecution does not object to describing the mental state requirement under Article 4 of the Statute as a special or particular or maybe even specific intent requirement; and thirdly, some remarks on the approach of interpretation taken in section 4(B) of our brief. I estimate that it will take approximately 20 to 22 minutes to complete my remarks. Your Honours, I proceed to the first set of observations. The Prosecution does not ask the Appeals Chamber to change the international law of genocide. The Prosecution is seeking a clarification from the Appeals Chamber of the requisite mental state standard under Article 4 in response to two propositions placed before the Chamber in paragraph 4.9, in paragraph 4.9, of the Prosecution brief. I'm referring to categories (b) and (c) in paragraph 4.9. The first proposition which we find in category (b) is as follows: The Prosecution submits that if an accused commits genocidal conduct consciously and with a will to act, and this accused knows that he is indeed destroying a group as such, then such an accused meets the mental state standard under Article 4 of the Statute. This proposition does not contain any element of probability. It refers to knowledge of the actual destruction, in whole or in part. The second proposition contained in category (c) in paragraph 4.9 is as follows: The Prosecution submits that if an accused who is an aider and abettor, who is an aider and abettor, to an ongoing objectively existing genocide, that is, a genocide that exists independently of the aider and abettor; and this accused commits his conduct of aiding and abetting consciously and with a will to act; and this accused knows that there is an ongoing genocide and that his conduct is a part of that genocide, but the accused only knows that the likely consequence of his conduct of aiding and abetting is a contribution to the ongoing genocide; the Prosecution submits in category (c) in paragraph 4.9 that such an accused meets the requisite mental state standard under Article 4 of the Statute. Categories (b) and (c) in paragraph 4.9 of our brief means what I have just described, nothing more. Any reference to “general intent” in section 4(B) of our brief and in paragraph 4(6) of our brief means only what I have now described in categories (b) and (c). Nothing else. Your Honours, both categories (b) and (c) assume that the accused committed the genocidal conduct or, if you like, the actus reus consciously and with will to act. That is, the mental state in both categories (b) and (c) contains two aspects: The first is the narrow mens rea directly relevant to the genocidal conduct of the accused which must have both a cognitive and volitive component. If you like, the accused must have committed the conduct consciously, which refers to the cognitive component, and with a will to act, which refers to the volitive component, that of volition. The second aspect of the mental state is the wider mental state of destroying a group as such which requires, in the submission of the Prosecution, at least a cognitive component. That could be knowledge of actual destruction being caused in whole or in part by the accused or, alternatively, probable destruction in the form of destruction as a likely consequence. In other words, Your Honours, there must be both a cognitive and a volitive component in the mental state of a person accused of genocide in the view of the Prosecution. Insofar as an accused has only one mind and normally one relevant mental state, the Prosecution submits that it is not necessary for the applier of the law to determine which aspect of the mental state the volitive component refers to. As a matter of fact, it may not be possible to do so. In reality, the mental state is one, and its different components merge. The Trial Chamber's position on the requisite mental state under Article 4 of the Statute appears to be that only dolus specialis meets the test. If that is the case, the Prosecution respectfully submits that the Trial Chamber erred. In any event, as my learned colleague Mr. Nice will explain when I have completed my remarks, the accused Goran Jelisic in this case met the higher standard of dolus specialis. In a nutshell, the question before the Appeals Chamber is whether the mental state of the accused, which must contain a cognitive and a volitive component with regard to the actus reus, must also contain a volitive component with regard to the mental state to destroy a group as such, and not only a cognitive component. In other words, does Article 4 of the Statute protect against genocidal conduct when the accused had the desire or purpose to destroy a group as such, but not against such conduct when the accused knew that he was indeed destroying the group or that the likely consequence was contribution to an ongoing destruction ? “Conscious desire” does not always require knowledge that the destruction is occurring or is a likely consequence, but the accused must, under the Motion of “conscious desire”, know that he desires. That is the cognitive component in the notion “conscious desire” in the view of the Prosecution. Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that the cynical mind that knows is as dangerous, if not more, than that which desires destruction. The mind that knows is normally the mind that knows how you bring about the result; the executive mind, if you like. This brings me to my second set of observations. The Prosecution does not object to the use of the terms "special intent" or "particular intent" or maybe even "specific intent" in describing the mental statement requirement under Article 4. The Prosecution cautions against any attempt to dilute or undermine the mental state requirement for genocide. But the reason why the mental state requirement under Article 4 is special is not because of the use of the word "intent" but because of the use of the words "destroy" and "group" and the two combined. It is special because of the particular combination of the two concepts. The wording of Article 4 says "destroy," Your Honours, not attack, discriminate, or persecute. It says "group as such", not civilian population, non-combatants, or just civilians. No other international crime within the Statute of the Tribunal contains these two words and/or their combination. They make the mental state requirement under Article 4 special, not the word "intent." However, whereas the words "destroy" and "group" refer to the scope of the mental state, if you like, what the mind must contain, the question before the Appeals Chamber in this appeal concerns the degree or quality of the mental state under Article 4, if you like, what the balance and degree of cognitive and volitive aspects of the mental state must be. If you like, the degree of intent refers to the light of the mind whilst the term scope of intent refers to what that light must be directed at. This distinction is well established in criminal legal theory, at least in some civil law countries, and the Prosecution submits that it flows necessarily from a reasonable reading of the logical construction of the mental state formulation in Article 4 of the Statute. That brings me to the third set of observations which go to the approach of interpretation taken in the Prosecution's submission in section 4(B). The Prosecution submits that the mental state formulation in Article 4 does not mean only dolus specalis. This position rests on a combined textual, teleological, and logical contextual interpretation of Article 4. These approaches to interpretation are rooted in customary international law as expressed in Article 31 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, which we can apply, at least by analogy, as confirmed in Tribunal jurisprudence. Let us look at the three approaches briefly. The logical contextual approach is: as explained in my previous sets of observations: The word "intent" in Article 4 must be interpreted in its context and its context is i"ntent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such." It is that context which provides for the speciality of the mental state under Article 4. The words "destroy" and "group" combined make this a distinct mental state different from all other international crimes. Secondly, a teleological interpretation of Article 4 of the Statute provides that Article 4's mental state requirement cannot just be dolus specalis. As to the exact object and purpose of the 1948 Genocide Convention from which Article 4 of the Statute is taken, I quote from the 1951 Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice on reservations to the Genocide Convention: "The Convention was manifestly adopted for a purely humanitarian and civilising purpose. It is indeed difficult to imagine a convention that might have this dual character to a greater degree, since its object on the one hand is to safeguard the very existence of certain human groups and on the other to confirm and endorse the most elementary principles of morality. In such a convention the contracting States do not have any interests of their own ; they merely have, one and all, a common interest, namely, the accomplishment of those high purposes which are the raison d'etre of the Convention." The continued existence of human groups may be the highest legal interest which the international legal order recognises. The Prosecution submits that an interpretation of Article 4 of the Statute, which restricts the mental state requirement to just dolus specalis will undermine the object and purpose of Article 4 and the Genocide Convention. It could even significantly reduce the deterrent function of that Convention. Thirdly, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that also a contextual interpretation of the word "intent" in Article 4 provides that it is not just dolus specalis that falls within its scope. The ordinary meaning of intent, as opposed to the technical legal meaning which one might have in some national jurisdictions, is not dolus specalis. This is the case in at least three of the equally authentic languages of the Genocide Convention, English, French, and Spanish. I repeat, it is not the technical legal usage that matters. This position taken by the Prosecution is not a manifestation of hypertextual speculative interpretation; far from it. Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that either of these three approaches to interpretation, certainly if they are combined, would support the Prosecution's submission that the mental state formulation of Article 4 does not only mean dolus specalis, but that categories (b) and (c) in 4.9 of the Prosecution brief fall within Article 4 as well. It is the position of the Prosecution that it is not necessary to resort to supplementary means of interpretation to reach this conclusion. The conclusion is reasonable and it falls squarely within the limits of the principle of nullum crimen sine lege. If the Court were to find it necessary to resort to supplementary means of interpretation, the Prosecution submits that such sources should recognise the distinction between the scope and degree of mental state in order to be directly relevant to the question before the Chamber. Furthermore, if any sources are in effect inconsistent with the object and purpose of Article 4 and the Genocide Convention, they cannot be given decisive weight alone or combined with other similar sources. There are time constraints which makes it difficult for me to review some of the supplementary sources that are in support of our position, but I simply refer to Article 30 of the ICC Statute, the ICC elements of crimes document relevant to genocide, and the final report of the Commission of Experts. We also have support in the published writings, or about to be published writings, at least in one case, of eminent academics with recognised expertise in the field, and I am referring to, inter alia, Professor Triffterer and Professor Gil Gil. In conclusion, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber's judgement appears to suggest that only a normal person with a genocidal motive and knowledge of a genocidal plan can meet the mental standard under Article 4. Where does that leave the cynical, willing executioner without whom genocides do not and cannot occur? The Appeals Chamber should not, we respectfully submit, provide a restrictive precedent on the scope of mental state under Article 4 which would leave the cynical willing executioners beyond the reach of the Statute and the Genocide Convention. Your Honours, the leap from proof of knowledge to proven desire or purpose must not become a black hole through which the object and purpose of Article 4 and the Genocide Convention is drained. In short, the case of the Prosecution is, in three points: One, the Court may refer to the mental state requirement under Article 4 as 9 “special” or “particular” because of the words "destroy" and "group" and their combination in the actual wording of the Article. Two, the Court should not and need not lower the mental state requirement for genocide under Article 4. It simply needs to give effect to the unique words of "destroy" and "group" in light of the object and purpose of the provision and the Genocide Convention. Three, the Chamber should hold that categories (b) and (c) in paragraph 4.9 of the Prosecutor's brief meet the mental state requirement of Article 4 of the Statute; that is, categories (b) and (c) as they are expressed in the brief and as they have been explained by me in my remarks today. That concludes my initial observations, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Counsel, I wonder if you would clarify one thing for me. There are several commentators, expert commentators on genocide, with whom I'm sure you're familiar, who have suggested that knowledge is sufficient. That would be your, roughly your categories (b) and (c). In other words, knowledge that one's intentional acts will bring about the consequences of destruction, in whole or in part, of the designated group, or your (c) goes beyond that into likely consequences. Do you identify yourself or affiliate yourself with that point of view that knowledge of the consequences, the consequences being destruction of the group in whole or in part, is sufficient; or there is another group of commentators which suggest that from that degree of knowledge one can infer intent?

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is not putting forward a general position on knowledge vis-à-vis the mental state requirement in Article 4. It is only suggesting that categories (b) and (c) in paragraph 4.9, that is in the circumstances that I described, knowledge of actual destruction suffices- and in category (c), for an aider and abettor, and only for an aider and abetter, knowledge that the likely consequence of your conduct is a contribution to an ongoing, objectively existing genocide which the aider and abetter has knowledge of and in the case where the aider and abettor knows that his conduct is a part of that independently existing genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So just to follow up, and I'll complete it. I understand the purport of your argument. I understand this is not particularly this case, but the purport of your argument would be that if one had no bad feelings or enmity against a particular group, but that -- but knew that what the actor was going to do was, in fact, going to destroy, in whole or in part the group, he was completely neutral about his feelings about the group, he was doing it for a completely different reason to get a hold of the territory, whatever, he didn't care about the group, but knew that the consequences of his action would be to destroy Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the group, then that would satisfy your interpretation of Article 4, genocide?

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Not exactly, Your Honour. You used the words "would be" and category (b) does not contain any element of probability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: It is higher than the standard of Article 30 of the ICC Statute. It refers to a knowledge of an actual result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. But you have no, you have no need for, in either (b) or (c), any evil motive, any enmity between the actor and the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: The position of the Prosecution is that in a strict sense, there need not in categories (b) and (c) be a volitive component in the mind of the perpetrator. He need not desire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: -- the result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Bergsmo, may I ask you this question: Your submissions arise, really, out of the reference by the Trial Chamber to the concept of dolus specialis. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, should I take it that that term applies to the mental state of the accused and looks to an especially high degree of his volition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: I can only answer yes to the second part of your question because, again, it is the submission of the Prosecution that what makes the mental state requirement under Article 4 special is not the degree required or the quality of intent required, but it is the references to the words "destroy" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I'm speaking abstractly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Without reference to the particular terminology in the Statute, you see, does dolus specialis normally pertain to the mental state of the accused, and does it look to a specially high degree of his volition?

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: It refers to the mental state of the accused, and for the purposes of our submission in section 4(B), we have referred to dolus specialis as “conscious desire” or the act of consciously desiring, and whether that is a particularly high degree of mental state is not clear. I don't think there is a recognised definition of the term "dolus specialis" in international criminal law. Neither is there a general principle of law, we would submit, that enjoys support in national jurisdictions from all the main legal traditions that would give us a clear definition of the term "dolus specialis." But clearly, by using the English version "conscious desire," we are referring to a clear volitive component in that mental state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Is it possible to read the judgement this way: All right, the Trial Chamber referred to the concept of dolus specialis, but in context, was it referring to the state of mind of the actor, or was it referring to intent in relation to the forbidden -- the specifically forbidden acts? Can there be a distinction between two things, a specific intent in the sense of an intent to do specifically forbidden acts, and a special intent in the sense of a particular state of mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Yes. This is what we have referred to as the two aspects of the mental state, and we are suggesting that for the genocidal conduct, the actus reus, there must be both a cognitive and volitive 9 component;whereas for the broader mental state, bringing about the destruction of the group as such, there need only be a cognitive component in the submission of the Prosecution. If one applies the term "dolus specialis" in the meaning of conscious desire, it would seem that the desire, the volitive component, would only refer to the bringing about of a destruction, in whole or in part, of the group. But as I said earlier, it would seem to the Prosecution that in reality, since we are talking about one mind and one mental state of the accused, the different components of the mental state will merge into one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg or his predecessor has pointed out, I think, that that term occurred only once in the judgement. What would you say to this question: Is it possible to read the judgement in a way which says this, that the Trial Chamber in referring to the concept of dolus specialis was really referring to a specific intent to commit the specifically forbidden acts and was not referring to any particular state of mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: It would seem to the Prosecution that a specific intent to commit certain acts is a manifestation of the mind of the accused. And if the Trial Chamber used the term "dolus specialis" to describe the fact that the accused had to have committed the actus reus with will to act, and the Trial Chamber is not requiring that there be a desire or a conscious desire with regard to bringing about the result of destruction, then it would seem that the Trial Chamber -- the view of the Trial Chamber was in accordance with the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. That is all the assistance I need. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: I will then give the floor to my learned colleague and friend, Mr. Geoffrey Nice, who will address the other aspects of section 4 of the Prosecution brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have asked that you may have available to you for the purposes of my submissions not only the judgement of the Court, but also the annex to our brief. It's not the public format, but I am alert to the initials of all the witnesses who gave evidence in closed session, so I will not offend the rules of the Tribunal in drawing your attention to passages within that annex. And it is my function today to deal with, to the degree necessary, the facts of or evidence in the case. And I put it in that way because, of course, all these arguments are without prejudice to our basic submission that the flawed procedures in themselves require that the case should be reheard. But nevertheless, because we cannot know how the Chamber will resolve its decisions, we make such arguments as we can to assist at this stage. The Chamber may think, and it is my submission, that it is appropriate not only to look at the material, the evidence, in the case, but also to focus on the process whereby the Trial Chamber dealt with the evidence. For if and insofar as it is clear that the process was flawed, why, then, the more flawed the process, the less weight it would be appropriate for this Chamber to place on the Trial Chamber's decision and the more impossible it is, in our submission, to sustain that conclusion.
