These cases, of course, as we've seen, pass from lawyer to lawyer, and I'm happy to be here to provide some aspect of continuity, for although I did not start the case - it was started by Mr. Teree Bowers - I took it over at a very early stage with Mr. Vladimir Tochilovsky and saw it through to its conclusion, and that gives me, if appropriate in due course, the opportunity to assist the Chamber in response to such complaints made by the accused in respect of the Trial Chamber's conduct as may still be being maintained. But at this stage of the argument, can I make the point that must have been obvious to this Chamber itself, namely, that in and insofar as there is material to show that the Trial Chamber was overconcerned with matters of timetable as revealed in the Defence complaints, why, of course, those matters lend some support to our very great concerns about what happened here in the improper, the wrongful abbreviation of the full process. Your Honours, for a case of this general type, there will be categories of evidence, and, loosely, you will be looking for evidence of what's been done generally of which the defendant's acts may be a part, then you will be concerned with the evidence of what the accused himself did, and, finally, you will be concerned with evidence of his state of mind. In this case, there was a very substantial quantity of material in all three categories. Indeed, the very quantity of material, its clarity and its strength, the Chamber may conclude, would have made this the case of a willing, but as it is sometimes described, low-level execution to be tried for genocide, for rarely in the case of such a potential accused could the evidence have been so complete. And as the Chamber knows, the decision to charge with genocide was made by the Prosecutor, Justice Arbour, confirmed by a member, indeed, of this Chamber, and on evidence that was not only in accordance with what was then presented but more substantial in various respects. And many lawyers and judges might have relished the opportunity of discussing the law and facts of a case, although that pleasure could not, of course, in itself justify the bringing of such a case. But as the Chamber knows - and these are the conclusion of my opening remarks - but as the Chamber knows more materially, the surviving victims and the bereaved and the others in the Brcko area and elsewhere who may use the word "genocide" to describe their suffering, have a legitimate interest and had a legitimate interest and expectation in this case being fully and openly litigated. And as we approach the process of dealing with the facts, the significance of which I have already pointed, the Chamber may want to have at least in mind that when it was clear that the Trial Chamber was about to make a final determination, the Prosecution alerted it, by its motion of the 15th of October, 1999, to the difficulties it was facing and the problems it might encounter. I don't know if the Chamber has had an opportunity to consider that particular motion, but I can summarise for you its effect. Not only did it remind the Trial Chamber that 98 bis was new, that the Prosecution had been given no indication of the Trial Chamber's concerns, not only did it notify the Trial Chamber of the need to hear argument and of the necessarily incomplete state of the Prosecution's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what limb are you on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These are my introductory remarks, and they touch, as I suggested, on this issue, but I'll repeat it because I may not have made it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'll tell you why I ask the question. I see from this guidance sheet passed to us this morning by Mr. Yapa that you would be speaking to us of the evidence relating to the genocidal intent of Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to do that, but I hope I'm going to be forgiven if it's a little wider than that, because I'm dealing with the facts and the approach to facts quite generally, because for reasons that I hope will become clear, it's our submission that the Chamber has not only got to consider the evidence, the material, but it's got to consider the approach for the reason I advanced a few minutes ago about a flawed approach undermining the value that could be placed by this Appeals Chamber on the Trial Chamber's approach and decision. Just briefly returning to the motion of the Prosecution of the 15th of October, 1999, not knowing what the Trial Chamber's concerns were but having to do our best to assess what might have been at stake, they were specifically alerted to the test being the test not of satisfaction beyond reasonable doubt. It's set out in the October 15th motion. It was suggested that there was no reason to distinguish between level of participants in a chain of authority as between those who were and those who were not vulnerable to the charge of genocide. They were alerted to the case of Nikolic, in this court, and they were alerted to complicity in genocide being, in the argument of the Prosecution, closely identifiable to aiding and abetting for which the defendant had been tried. So it was with that forewarning that the Chamber took the course it did, the Prosecution having made it quite clear that our case was incomplete. Now, Your Honours, I turn to what actually happened and then we'll look at some of the evidence together, if we may. Of course we say that they applied the wrong test to the evidence. And as we look at the evidence in certain areas, Your Honours may find that an irresistible conclusion because it can only be a simple case of there being no case to answer when there is simply no evidence on a particular topic. A routine burglary, no evidence that the accused is the burglar. It doesn't matter how the judge, at the end of the Prosecution case, describes the test he applies, one way or another, no evidence that it's the man. No case; the case must stop. That's simply not the situation here. In all areas, a very considerable body of material. It may be susceptible to arguments going one way or another, but material upon which on any reckoning a Tribunal properly directing itself could have reached the conclusion that the Prosecution was going to invite the Tribunal to reach. So that it's either a question, as I hope to persuade you, that they inevitably applied the wrong test or alternatively that they simply failed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Nice, you're going back to terrain already traversed by previous speakers, I believe. Is that your intention?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, it's not, but I'll move on. Can I, nevertheless, and I hope you will permit me this, just this observation, if it's helpful, because I heard Judge Wald's concern about the difference between a jury trial and a judge alone trial and why the test should be the test that we say on the authority of this Tribunal it is, and can I respectfully remind those of the Court with this experience that not only in Magistrate's Court for which is an authority, but where judges alone in non-criminal cases, for example, in the United Kingdom and, as I understand it but haven't been able to confirm, in other countries such as the Cameroon where judges alone try criminal cases, the courts will not entertain insufficiency arguments in the absence of an election to call no evidence because to entertain sufficiency arguments risks prejudgement, pre-evaluation, and takes the court down a road that it is difficult to return. And I hope you may find that helpful. The evidence before the Chamber, and now I come directly, subject to one other observation that I want to make, the evidence before the Chamber on which they acted did not include evidence upon which they subsequently sought to rely in their written judgement. The Chamber will have in mind that substantial reliance was placed by the Trial Chamber on the psychiatric evidence. That evidence was not before them at the time -- as evidence. Indeed, it substantially wasn't before them at all at the time they gave their oral judgement. It was evidence that was only ever laid before them in the course of the sentencing exercise that came much later, and it was, therefore, wrong for them to incorporate that evidence as material upon which they could found their decision in respect of genocide. Further, the evidence, even when it was before them, was not before them for the purpose or on the topic in respect of which they placed reliance. Not at all. The evidence said nothing about the accused's state of mind, intention, anything else at the time he committed the killings he did, and it spoke of other matters, fitness to stand his trial and, to a limited extent, risk of being a danger in the future. Then can I -- as we look at the evidence, can I very respectfully distinguish for Your Honours and perhaps for all of us the differences between the exercise that if you decide you have to -- have to perform this exercise Your Honours perform and the exercise that would have been performed by the Trial Chamber had it heard representations in answer to whatever its concerns may have been. A Trial Chamber considering the sufficiency of a case at the end of a criminal Prosecution, has three parties, judges or judge and counsel, all of whom have direct experience of the evidence which, by the process of argument, they can revive in their memories. Those of us with experience in these cases will know that the process of argument revives the recollection of the evidence, stimulates first in the mind of the opposing counsel counter-arguments, and all too frequently, in the minds of neutral judges, questions. They're not put as arguments. They're always raised as issues, but nevertheless. And that makes the evidence that is being assessed three dimensional. Here, alas, at best, if everybody had read all the transcripts, the assessment would be two dimensional because Your Honours would not have any direct recollection of the evidence to revive and any direct potential for assessment of the witnesses beyond the way they appear in writing. So that this exercise, in our respectful submission, is radically different from the exercise that should have been conducted. Finally, when a sufficiency argument has been advanced and dealt with by a first instance trial court, its deliberations and the arguments addressed to it are then available for the appeal court or chamber to review. It can discover what has been taken into account by way of evidence and by way of argument, and it can then, subject to its own limitations, according to which jurisdiction it's in, it can then exercise a review. Here, this Chamber has no material of that type to work on and has only the judgement, and it is to that judgement that I would take you and also to the annex to our brief. In the English version of the judgement, at page 20 and at paragraph 65, as the Court will recall, the Trial Chamber noted that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. material element of the crime of genocide had been satisfied, and, therefore, we don't need to trouble you in respect of that element. Likewise on page 24 at paragraph 77, it found discriminatory intent had been established, and I need trouble you no further with evidence in relation to that. As to the remaining pages, as the Chamber will know, we have presented in narrative form in our brief the arguments, and there's no need for me to repeat those because that will waste your time and I know you will have read them already; rather, I'll take you, if I may, through the remaining paragraphs of the judgement which are the ones that are material, make some observations about the arguments or the propositions that the Trial Chamber advanced, and through annex A to our brief, take you to some of the evidence and show you what has been so manifestly overlooked. But this is, starting at page 24, within the overall heading of the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the group as such. Can I first of all take Your Honours to page 26 for one observation on the evidence. It's towards the foot of the page and it's at the end of the paragraph where the Chamber said: "Genocidal intent may therefore be manifest in two forms. It may consist of desiring the extermination of a very large number of the members of the group in which case it would constitute an intention to destroy a group en masse; however, it may also consist of the desired destruction of a more limited number of persons selected for the impact that their disappearance would have upon the survival of the group as such. This would then constitute an intention to destroy the group selectively." The Prosecutor did not actually choose between these two options, and if that as an issue had been raised, the reply would have been that both were possible on the evidence for a very substantial proportion was aimed at and, on the evidence, kill; but in any event, the lesser, much more focussed killing pattern was overwhelmingly revealed. If we then turn over to -- I can turn over several pages, I think, to page 29, there are three paragraphs, 91, 92, and 93, which deal with lists. And it may be, and it's hard to tell because there is no argument that can explain it, it may be that there was fundamental confusion by the Trial Chamber in what lists it was concerned with. Certainly that's one possible interpretation of these paragraphs. May I explain the evidential position? There was a great deal of evidence, and I'm going to take you to it very shortly, about lists, bits of paper with names on them that were given both to the accused and, on the evidence, to others, those lists being the names of people to be processed, in reality, to be killed. Separate from those lists and within the evidence-gathering exercise for the trial, there were lists of people whose bodies had been found in the mass grave, 200 plus names were provided by the authorities of which 100 could be named, could be identified; there was a list of 39 names provided by a former figure of authority within the community, being the names of prominent people whom he was satisfied had disappeared, necessarily killed; and there was another larger list prepared showing municipality Muslim leaders, the vast percentage of whom, half, were shown to have been killed, the other half being people whom on the evidence had fled. And within those lists, the 39 and the 100 named from such mass graves had been found, there were names of people who, on the evidence and, indeed, by his admission, the accused was the executioner. So the lists are entirely different. The evidential lists went to show overwhelmingly that the important leaders of the local Muslim community had been targeted for execution and had been executed. The other lists of which the accused spoke in his interview with investigators and of which other witnesses spoke, were lists provided them at the time to commit the acts that they then committed. And if one reads, and I don't desire to do it in full now, paragraphs 91 to 93, it is at least arguable that there is confusion completely in the minds of the Trial Chamber. However, if one looks at paragraph 93 more particularly, it says this: "The reason for being on these lists and how they were compiled is not clear. It hasn't been established that the accused relied on such a list in carrying out the executions." And there's a reference to Jelisic seeming to select names of persons at random from a list. It then suggests that there's no evidence, or it hasn't been established -- and again, the use of the words like "establish" this Chamber may think fit, as in so many cases, with our contention that the Trial Chamber was applying the final proof-beyond-reasonable-doubt test rather than saying to itself, "There is no material that could establish." I'll hope not to repeat that argument except when it is so obvious I can't overlook it, but it recurs. Not only had it been established that the lists seen by Witness K or another witness correspond to that submitted by the Prosecutor, and then this conclusion: "It is therefore not possible to conclude beyond all reasonable doubt that the choice of victims arose from a precise logic to destroy the most representative figures of the Muslim community." Same argument about proof. And if the Chamber would be good enough to go to the schedule or the annex at page 21, I'm not going to go over many entries. If I can point you to where the entries are and invite you to look at some of them, I trust I shall have performed my duty. But at 21 -- I beg your pardon, 29 first, my mistake, page 29 first on the lists, you'll see first on page 29, and the Chamber will know from what we've said that scheduling of evidence was always going to be helpful to the Trial Chamber. We prepared a schedule in advance at the end of the Prosecutor's case. We weren't able to help them with it. It was there. We prepared another one for the sentencing exercise, and this is one for Your Honours we hope have helped. And one of the features of the case, it may be, was that the defendant had given very substantial answers in interview, wittingly or unwittingly, and that material not only provided evidence against himself, it is evidence of the facts that he admits. Very little of this seems to have been referred to by the Trial Chamber in detail, and sometimes at all. So on page 29 there are excerpts from the transcript of the interview where, for example, the accused said, page 8, and I'll be as quick as I can with these, that he was given a list. They were prominent people. That's the only way to describe them. Nothing could be clearer than that the targeting by lists was of prominent people. Page 17, when dealing with people who he killed first, from -- he killed at certainly two sites, the police station and then subsequently at the Luka camp, and at the police station it was the people from cell 13. And he says this, they had been on "the" lists, because he spoke of being given lists right at the beginning when he was recruited before the bridges were blown and the conflict was initiated. Page 22, "99 per cent of the people from the lists I had seen were Muslim." Page 47, "It was a list of Muslim prisoners, and at the end, it had the Crisis Staff printed on it." So this was a list with authority to him. Page 49 asked about the list. His answer, "Each of our conversations from the named person having been told that as many Muslims as possible had to be killed and that Brcko should become a Serbian town." Over the page, and I'm going to ask, if I may, that the Tribunal -- the Chamber looks at these documents itself, because otherwise I'll take more time than I will have, but it goes on. There can be no doubt about the lists that he was provided and the purpose for which they were provided. But if you go on page 31, it was not just from the mouth of the defendant himself that these lists were spoken of. There's a Witness H. Many witnesses had pseudonyms, and only a limited number were in fully closed session. Witness H was able to speak of those 20 people recognised on both lists, and he spoke of their common Bosniak characteristic. There's another witness dealt with at the foot of the page whom I won't name or identify in any way, but the Chamber can see the effect of what that witness said. And at page 33, another witness - again I shan't name him - the second witness down, and so on. So that the, in our respectful submission to this Chamber, the conclusion in paragraph 93 is simply unsustainable where it says on any test, whichever test, it is not possible to conclude beyond reasonable doubt, there is no evidence that could go forward - whichever way we seek to interpret those words - that the choice of victims arose from a logic to destroy the most representative figures of the Muslim community. There was an enormous amount of material, further confirmed as you will find at page 21 in your schedule. I have lost my own page 21 by detaching it from the papers, sorry. Will Your Honours just give me a minute. I've managed to confuse my papers in a way I shouldn't have done. Well, at page 21, Your Honours will find the beginning of a category -- you'll find the beginning of a category of evidence summarised as singling out prominent Muslims. It goes on in this particular formulation of our schedule until page 28. If you look at the defendant's own answers in interview in the middle of that page, he starts identifying victims by their role within the Muslim party. He says further at the foot of the page how people were targeted because, second line from the bottom, they were high up in the SDA hierarchy, and his answers continue over the page. On page 22 there's the witness referred to in the middle of the page. It's dealt with in argument. It's the clearest possible evidence from somebody who had no reason to make it up or get it wrong, but what she saw or what was seen was evidence of the targeting of prominent Muslim people. And again, if the Court would be good enough at its time to look at the remainder of those pages -- let's see if there's anything in particular that I wanted to draw to your attention within them. Yes, I think I've already referred to what you can find on page 27 where, again, he says that the list he was given was of prominent people. So paragraph 93 in our respectful submission is totally flawed. And paragraph 94, over the page in the judgement, speaks of people reputedly released on the day of their arrival. The Chamber will have seen from the way the schedule has been prepared that the right-hand column says whether the evidence summarised has been dealt with at all in the judgement of the Court. Now, on pages 11 to 12 of this document, Your Honours will see in the evidence of a witness, Witness A, who had a pseudonym but whose evidence was otherwise public, that he said this right at the foot of the page, to take it quickly: "Despite the passes that were issued by the police, these passes were just a false hope for those who received them. They would get them today, they'd go home, and then the next day they would be brought back, either as we already heard from the stories of others who brought them then, they would be released in the morning and killed in the evening in their own homes or in the apartments or flats." This evidence, as are entry or non-entry in the right-hand column reveals, simply overlooked by the Chamber or not dealt with, and yet a fundamental and important piece of evidence about what was actually underlying the apparent or seeming release of individuals. So paragraph 94, flawed. Evidence to entirely the contrary effect to that upon which the Chamber sought to rely. Paragraph 95 asserts this, that it hadn't been established beyond all reasonable doubt, same argument, whether the accused killed Luka camp under orders. It goes on to say he presented himself as the Luka camp Commander, believed that he was the chief or at least a person in authority because he gave orders to the soldiers at the camp who appeared to be afraid of him. Well, if we'd been given an opportunity of considering that as an argument, we would have said it is perfectly clear on all the evidence, including the evidence of the defendant in interview, that he was doing what he was doing, including killing, pursuant to the overall plan, including the lists of which he had spoken and which the Chamber seems not to have regarded as of significance. In any event, the question of whether he killed all or only partly pursuant to orders is in no sense determinative of the issue in this case, (A) because what might matter would be the killings pursuant to orders, and there was a mass of evidence with regard to those; and secondly, because if architects of genocide choose to put in camps people who, however they've been recruited, however their proclivity has been identified, are people who will willingly kill even beyond the immediate instructions, that's not evidence that there was no genocide, very much the reverse. And in respect of this paragraph, paragraph 95, can I invite the Chamber, if it feels it could, to at least note the pages that it might want to consider from the schedule that touch on this, and then I will say for individual examples, probably take you to very few items. At page 35, you can start with the subcategory of material. Let's just look at the first of those entries on page 35 where indeed the defendant asserted on page 7 of one of his interviews that he was not killing by ethnicity but by order, something reflected in the next entry with the first lines of his answer. He was following a script by which he meant that when he killed someone, he killed them in the same way. This is all at the police station. And I must remember to say something more about those particular killings before I conclude. It goes on over the page to deal with further evidence on the same topic, and you can see, for example, on page 37 where the accused, in a long answer about killings of particular people, sets out quite a detailed account of how for those two particular victims others were giving him instructions and somebody else wanted to join in and commit a killing himself and so on. And you will find a great deal of evidence between here and page 41. On page 40, the matter was most succinctly summarised in an answer to the Presiding Judge. It came from a witness, Witness I, and the Presiding Judge asked the witness:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he give you the impression of directing the operations or of simply being someone who carried things out? A I could say that he was both. This is somebody who was there. A He carried out orders, but he also selected his victims through his own free will. He could have not shot dead someone even if he were told to do so, but he did quite a few things on his own. No reference to this in the judgement, as with so much of this material. Going on from page 41 to page 44, there is an interesting passage that's relied upon by the Chamber again overlooking the critical evidence. At the top of page 43, Witness A spoke of how there had come a time, after a couple of weeks, when somebody, apparently in a position of superior authority, stopped the killings, and this was relied upon by the Chamber as of significance. But what they didn't deal with is what Your Honours can see here at page 43, where Witness B says what he says there, but you'll also find that in our brief, at paragraph 467, the evidence was given by Mr. Ralston that the succession of killings at Brcko was not as a result of a decision by those organising things to stop of their own free will but because knowledge of what was happening at Brcko had seeped out and was in the public domain and that it was now no longer acceptable for this method of killing to be continued. So far from this evidence overall helping the accused in any way by showing that he was acting at random or acting beyond control, the evidence as a block - and there is a great deal more of it between pages 59 of this schedule and the end - shows, yes, he was acting pursuant to a plan because he was acting pursuant to orders. The evidence is from all sources, is varied, but, overall, consistent. So, yes, he was acting pursuant to orders, and he was killing. utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: May I deal firstly with ground 1 of the Prosecution's appeal. Complaint is made that they were not permitted to present argument before verdict, the Court having indicated that it was minded to give judgement following the close of the Prosecution case. I have formed the view that the Prosecution is, in fact, right in asserting that they ought to have been given leave to present a closing argument. Rule 86(A) appears to cover the position. It reads: "After the presentation of all the evidence, the Prosecutor may present a closing argument." Clearly, in the light of the course of action proposed by the Trial Chamber, all the evidence had concluded at the time they made their application to be heard, and I concede that on a strict reading of Rule 86, they ought to have been permitted to address the Chamber. Even were it not for the words Rule 86, I would have inclined to the view that the parties ought to have an opportunity to address a Trial Chamber before verdict, particularly if the verdict was to be adverse to the party who was seeking to address the court. It is, nonetheless, our submission that the failure of the Trial Chamber to permit the Prosecution the right of presenting an argument does not in any way invalidate the verdict. It is, one might say, at its height discourteous. It may be, indeed on a proper reading of Rule 86, almost certainly is contrary to the Rules of the Chamber, but they are fundamentally procedural. If on a proper analysis of the evidence the Prosecution fail on their third ground of appeal, which in our submission they ought, then we would submit that unfortunate though the error was in failing to allow them the right to be heard at the close of the evidence, that error in no way invalidates the verdict. Many years ago in England, a distinguished Judge, Lord Hewitt, said that justice must not only be done, it must be seen to be done. And by declining to hear one of the parties to the action, there is, we would submit, at least a perception that justice is not seen to be done if one of the parties is denied an opportunity to be heard. Therefore, we do not seek to sustain the approach adopted by the Trial Chamber. That does not, of course, concede that the appropriate remedy sought by the Prosecution, namely a retrial, ought to follow. It certainly cannot be, with respect to the submissions presented today, inevitable that a retrial follows, because that was the word that one time mattered. What Rule 117(C) says is in appropriate circumstances, the Appeal Chamber may order the accused be retried according to law. Those words import a discretion in the Appeal Chamber. There is contrary, to what has been argued, nothing inevitable about that consequence. And certainly if every procedural irregularity led inevitably to a retrial, we would submit there would be many more retrials than would be desirable. The words "in appropriate circumstances" in our submission can be substituted for the words "if justice demands." And we would submit that the answer to whether there needs to be a retrial in this case is to be found upon the Court's determination of the third ground of appeal. Put bluntly, it cannot be sensibly argued, can it, that if the Court actually came to the right decision by the wrong route there should be a retrial, with all the attendant cost and delay what that would entail, the ordeal of putting witnesses through the strain of giving evidence, and for that matter, the pressure on a defendant who has now been in custody for more than three years, all to achieve a result which, in our submission, the Court would have been driven to even had it heard the submissions of the Prosecution at the close of the evidence. It follows, therefore, that although I make the concession that they ought to have been given a right to be heard, we submit that no injustice flowed from that, and in fact the Court, the Trial Chamber, came to the correct decision, albeit by a shortened route. I ought, perhaps, at this early stage to indicate that although it was originally sought on behalf of the respondent to this appeal that a retrial be ordered, that is not a submission that I advance on his behalf today. The original brief filed on his behalf sought a retrial, despite the fact he had been acquitted of every count on the indictment that he contested. Were there to become fashionable, litigation need ever end. For the avoidance of doubt, we do not seek a retrial. We submit that the Trial Chamber came to the correct conclusion, albeit by the wrong route. As to the second ground of appeal, may I make my position clear. Insofar as the Trial Chamber applied the test of being satisfied beyond reasonable doubt to the determination of that decision at that stage, then we would submit that that was the wrong test to apply. I had in mind, when making the concession that I did, primarily the written judgement of the Court which clearly expresses itself in terms in which a common lawyer would only interpret it, as applying that standard to the decision that they were then making. I frankly confess that in the short time that I have been instructed, I have not studied the oral judgement as carefully as the Appeal Chamber, and recognise that judges from a civil jurisdictional background might not express themselves with quite the same precision as a judge from a common law background. We would submit that if on a true reading of the oral and written judgement the test applied by the Trial Chamber was, one, expressed in the way that the Court expressed it earlier today, namely when it said that no reasonable tribunal of fact could be sure beyond reasonable doubt on that evidence, that would be applying the correct test at that stage of the proceedings. The distinction, if I may analyse it, is this: Under Rule 98(B) the crucial words contained in the rules read as follows, namely, that the conviction is insufficient to sustain a conviction. The crucial words are "to sustain." That means, and I choose the definition of the Oxford English dictionary, to uphold the validity of, to support as valid. Transposed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. into a legal framework, it would mean to survive examination on appeal. It implies not just a consideration of the merits of a verdict at trial level, but an implication that they would survive examination in this Chamber. Now, the Appeal Chamber in the appeal of Dusko Tadic recognised, and I quote from page 28, paragraph 64 of the judgement: "It is important to note that two judges, both acting reasonably, can come to different conclusions on the basis of the same evidence. It follows that a conviction can be sustained even if reasonable judges would have come to a different conclusion on the facts as long as the conclusion is one that could be reasonably arrived at, and that is, with respect, my analysis of the proper test to be applied at the Rule 98 stage. In other words, if a reasonable Trial Chamber considering the evidence could reasonably convict, then the Trial Chamber ought not to intervene and direct a verdict or return a verdict of not guilty subject to one matter that I will touch on in a moment." I do not subscribe to the theory that the Trial Chamber is obliged to permit the trial to proceed even if there is a scintilla of evidence which suggests guilt, but because that scintilla of evidence exists, it is not obliged to allow the trial to proceed, if, when looked at against the factual background of the case as a whole, no reasonable Trial Chamber could convict on that evidence. So, for example, you may have a case where cross-examination has effectively destroyed a witness for the Prosecution who perhaps provides identity on a crucial count. The effect of cross-examination may be to render the evidence of the witness totally unreliable in the view of the Trial Chamber. The fact that you could extract from that witness' evidence one sentence which when viewed in isolation would provide a prima facie case against an accused is no reason to permit the trial to proceed following the conclusion of the Prosecution's case, because the Trial Chamber is entitled to look at the whole of the evidence at that stage and not to say, "Is there any evidence of guilt?" but the different question, "Is there any evidence which a reasonable Trial Chamber, properly directing itself, could return a safe verdict?" It is that second test that certainly, in scheduled offences in Northern Ireland, judges sitting alone apply when trying allegations of terrorism, they sitting, of course, without a jury. The Prosecution have filed a case from Ontario, the Queen and Collins and Palfrey. In our submission, that case provides no support for the proposition that they advance. The difference there, as was identified this morning by the Court, is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, may I utter a word of caution. Words falling from the lips of the Presiding Judge are not to be attributable to the Court. It's that particular Judge's view only.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I am, of course, mindful of that, and I'm grateful for the correction. The reference, in fact, that I am alluding to in fact came from Her Honour Judge Wald when she was identifying the possible distinction where the trier of fact is also the -- the trier of fact is different from the trier of law. And there is, of course a distinction where you have in a common law jurisdiction trial by a jury, then you have no reasoned judgement on the facts at all. The judge sitting with a jury has no idea of what the jury's view of the facts are, and, therefore, he will or she will inevitably be more circumscribed at the close of the case for the Crown than a Tribunal that is both the decider of law and fact because the Trial Chamber or a judge sitting without a jury will know that they have already come to the firm conclusion that certain of the evidence is, in their judgement, unreliable. They will come to the conclusion that this evidence could not, in their judgement, persuade any reasonable trier of fact to convict. And there is, we submit, a distinction, because the alternative would, we submit, be somewhat absurd. Let's imagine that the extreme position be taken of the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber can hear a case. All three judges can say to themselves, "Well, there is no way that we would convict this man on this evidence. We don't believe that witness, we don't believe that witness, and we certainly don't believe the third." Are they to sit mute, while as in this case Mr. Greaves told the Trial Chamber he had 60 Defence witnesses he was proposing to call, 6-0. Sixty Defence witnesses were going to be called over a period of months before they could articulate that firm conclusion they had already reached. Now, it may be, we submit, a matter of substance more than -- a matter of form rather than substance that really lies behind the Prosecution complaint. Can I hypothesise for a moment? Let us suppose that the Presiding Judge, at the conclusion of the evidence in this case, had said to the Court, "It may help you both to know that we have, all three of us, come to the view that we could not possibly be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of this man's guilt having heard the evidence that we have." Now, there is nothing that precludes a judge from saying that. If he had said it in this case, could there be any complaint about the fact that he had said it? There may well be much complaint about the fact that they didn't agree with him, but that is the cut and thrust of advocacy. But there can be no complaint, surely, about a court indicating to the parties a view that they had formed, not at a preliminary stage but after the Prosecution have called all of the evidence that they want to on the issue. If they had done that, we would submit that no complaint could have been made, and we would be in exactly the same position today, only ground 2 of the appellant's grounds would be unarguable. In our submission, it is, in reality, a complaint of form over substance. I don't have any other submissions in relation to the first two grounds of appeal and propose to move to the Prosecutor's third ground. It is perhaps best encapsulated in the Prosecution brief which asserts at paragraph 4.7 that the plain, ordinary meaning of Article 4 does not support the proposition that dolus specialis, special intent, is required, and continues such a proposition also contradicts the Akayesu judgement and the jurisprudence of the ICTY. Now, in oral argument today, there has been a slight refinement of that submission as I understood it. There is, I think it is now conceded, a requirement for dolus specialis, in other words, a proposition directly contrary to what's in the written brief at paragraph 4.7, but that dolus specialis doesn't mean what everybody thinks it means but something else falling, when analysed, short of dolus specialis. In other words, what, as I understood it, the effect of the submission was, to concede the words, which as I will demonstrate would be difficult to explain away without concession, but to say, all right, the words are right, but it's the way they've been interpreted is wrong. We submit it's nothing more in reality than a rather clever attempt at a forensic sidestep. And I intend no disrespect when I say that, but on analysis that is, is it not, what was happening? In our submission, a special intent is necessary to prove the offence of genocide, and that was correctly identified by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 66 of its judgement, and it's perhaps worth seeing what the special intent was. The Trial Chamber said at paragraph 66: "It is in fact the mens rea which gives genocide its speciality and distinguishes it from an ordinary crime and other crimes against international humanitarian law. The undergoing crime or crimes must be characterised as genocide when committed with the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group as such. Stated otherwise, the prohibited act must be committed against an individual because of his membership in a particular group and as an incremental step in the overall objective of destroying the group. Two elements which may therefore be drawn from the special intent are: One, that the victims belong to an identified group, and two, that the alleged perpetrator must have committed his crimes as part of a wider plan to destroy the group as such. Acts committed against victims because of their membership in a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group, (A) the discriminatory nature of the acts, and then the special intent which characterises genocide supposes that the alleged perpetrator of the crime selects his victims because they are part of a group which he is seeking to destroy with the goal of the perpetrator or perpetrators of the crime is to destroy all or part of a group. It is the `membership' of the individual in a particular group rather than the identity of the individual that is the decisive criteria in determining the immediate victims of the crime of genocide." In our submission, that is a textbook definition of the crime. Put simply, to be guilty of genocide, it is not sufficient to kill your victim because he is a Muslim or a Jew or a Catholic. The killing must be accompanied by the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, or religious group. It is this state of mind which elevates that which would otherwise be a crime against humanity to the crime of genocide, which is the most serious of all crimes falling within the jurisdiction of this Court and is being called by academic lawyers the crime of crimes. Indeed, if we reflect for one moment about the jurisprudence on the offence of genocide stemming from the Second World War, we can see how it has developed as the international -- as an answer international law has given to the Holocaust which occurred in Nazi, Germany. There, of course, is the classic illustration of the offence of genocide being manifested by a state against a religious group. Diverting for one moment, no one could ever doubt for a moment that the authors of the "Final Solution" in the Third Reich were guilty of genocide. It is perhaps the most classic example. They had that special intent, namely, the objective of destroying the entire Jewish race, save for those few exceptions who, because of their special skills, were of value to the German state. It does not mean that each member of each Einstadt Gruppan and command unit was guilty of genocide who carried out the crime as those groups moved from town to town and from village to village throughout eastern Europe. They might or they might not be, depending upon what individual, personal intent they had. Many of them may not have had an intent personally to wipe out or to assist in the extermination of the entire Jewish race. The crime, we would submit with respect, whilst not confined to the architects of genocidal plans, is perhaps best illustrated as being an offence which is designed and can be applied to the people who are the architects of genocide in the sense that they are the decision-makers and the policy makers. Now, I am not seeking to say that one man on his own can't be guilty of genocide; he can be. There are considerable evidential difficulties to be overcome in so finding. And the Trial Chamber themselves accepted that one man could be guilty of genocide and addressed that issue very carefully in the course of their judgement. But as a crime, it is, we submit, most normally reserved, most usefully reserved for the architects of ethnic cleansing. The difference between a crime against humanity and the crime of genocide is only that state of mind. In our submission, there is a consistent acceptance of this requirement for special intent to be found throughout the judgements of this Court in the ICTY and also in the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. In the Rwanda case of Kayishema and Ruzindena, the Court there spoke, and I quote their words: "Of the unique element of special intent to destroy in whole or in part a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group as a prerequisite for the crime of genocide." And the it is found in paragraph 9 of the sentencing judgement. It is that unique element spoken to in the Kayishema and Ruzindena judgement the Trial Chamber, in the instant case, was alluding to. The Trial Chamber in the case of Serushago, another Rwanda case, used the same words as the Trial Chamber here did in defining genocide. The Trial Chamber in that case said, and I quote: "The crime of genocide is unique because its element of dolus specialis, special intent, which requires that the crime be committed with the intent to destroy in whole or in part a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group," to be found in paragraph 4 of the judgement, later referred to genocide as the crime of crimes. We broadly submit that the assertion in the written brief of the Prosecution that the Trial Chamber in the instant case departed from established jurisprudence in this Court or in the International Tribunal of Rwanda as, frankly, incapable of being sustained. We filed with my brief skeleton submission an article published in the International and Comparative Quarterly Review of July 2000 by Professor Verdirame of the University of Nottingham in England which addressed the divergent approaches to mens rea and the requirement of it for the crime of genocide. Page 584, it addresses the mental element and discusses both the Trial Chamber's decision in the case I've mentioned of Kayishema and Ruzidena, and the case of Akayseu which the Prosecution quoted in its appellate's brief and to which I will return in a moment. What the Professor said, at the top of page 588, is as follows: "This distinction between the different types of hostile intents against a group is of great importance. The intent to discriminate against or even to persecute a group cannot be considered identical to the intentional pursuit of its physical annihilation. In addition, a method for the judicial application of the dolus specialis in genocide has been crystallised by the ad hoc tribunals. First, contextual elements are assessed." It seems that I fused the lights of the building. I just pause for a moment. My eyesight is not good enough to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Is it something I said? I'll start the quotation again in the circumstances. "This distinction between different types of hostile intents against a group is of great importance.
