Now, in support of the Prosecution's submission that Article 4 does not require dolus specialis in the way that one has always understood it in the past, academic support is now prayed in aid in the form of the filing made two days ago. Now, I make no complaint about the lateness of it. We would invite the Court to consider with some care the views of the academics annexed to that filing to see whether on proper analysis it does support the proposition by the Prosecution at all. The first is a rough translation of part of a book by Alicia Gil Gil, and the rough translation that I have been provided with seems to accept, on page 258, when dealing with the mens rea, that it is necessary to prove that the person has the intention, the will to act, of continuing to kill, or in the case of various perpetrators, with the knowledge of the intention of the co-authors of continuing to kill until the completion of the plan - by that it can only mean the plan to exterminate the group in whole or in part - and at least counting on the possibility of dolus eventualis. Now, I'm not quite sure how that squares with the proposition as advanced by the Prosecution. A little later in the judgement, on a page that is unnumbered that follows page 258 in the faxed copy supplied to me, the author talks about the plan in these terms: "To inflict conditions which are abstractly capable of bringing about the result of extermination which includes the knowledge of such a risk." The second book is by way of a press release, because it has yet to be published, from Professor Triffterer at the University of Salzburg. I personally confess that I found the syntax and grammar something of a strain, which I'm sure reflects more on the translation than it does Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. on the good professor. But even there at page 1441, he talks about the need for an additional intent, although as translated, I confess it is not entirely easy to follow. What he is clearly arguing for in Annex 3, is a change in the law. What the good professor there says is that the need for a special intent as proposed in Article 6 of the Rome Statute should be eliminated. Well, the good professor, of course, is perfectly entitled to think that the law should be changed and to argue to that effect. It is, in effect, conceding that the law currently is not as he would like, and what he doesn't like about it is the special intent that is required. We would submit that there is much to be said in favour of the law being as it is. Anyway, I anticipate that this Court will be anxious to state the law as it is rather than as the good professor would like it to be. The only case quoted by the Prosecution in its written submission is the Rwanda judgement of Akayseu. The analysis of that judgement, in our submission, does nothing to support their argument. I quote from page 3: "The crime of genocide is unique because," and I add the words "it is," "of its element of dolus specialis, which requires that the crime be committed with the intent," and then it continues in what is now the familiar words. How that supports the proposition as adumbrated in the brief is, frankly, beyond me. The Akayseu judgement, as identified, was dealing with the difficulty in proving the special intent required for the crime of genocide. It wasn't saying, when you read that judgement, that there was no need for special intent. It was identifying the problem that you would have in proving it against an individual. And at paragraph 523 of their judgement they said, and I quote, "Intent is a mental factor which is difficult, even impossible, to determine," adding that, "failing a confession of the accused, intent can only be inferred from a certain number of presumptions of fact." While, with respect, the Trial Chamber I agree with the second part of their quotation, I do not, with respect, agree with the first. Intent as a mental factor is not difficult or even impossible to prove, and if that quote had general application, every trier of fact in domestic criminal jurisdictions, be they prefects, magistrates, judges, or jurists, would have difficulty in applying the criminal law to the facts of a very large number of crimes. In reality, the triers of fact in the criminal jurisdictions of the world have no difficulty in inferring intent by drawing safe conclusions from the evidence as a whole. Most jurisdictions require for the crime of murder either an intent to kill or an intent to cause serious harm. That intent is easily inferred by a judge from what the accused does. So I don't accept as a general application the proposition that intent as a mental factor is difficult or impossible to determine absent confession. Applying the crime of genocide to those who formulated the final solution in Nazi Germany would, I anticipate, not present the slightest difficulty to any lawyer in inferring the necessary intent for genocide. The commander of the concentration camps of Dachau and Belsen would likewise, I anticipate, have no difficulty in having intent inferred in cases were they to be brought to trial. Of course, evidentially, the lower down the command structure you get or the further removed sideways you get in government from the decision that leads to the ethnic cleansing, the more difficulties you may have in an individual case to prove intent; but that, we would submit, is just a reflection of the sort of evidential difficulties that are common in all jurisdictions. What the Trial Chamber in this case was referring to as the special intent for genocide was, we submit, something which in an appropriate case could be easy to infer from the evidence in the case, but clearly here, and perhaps not surprisingly here, was in fact impossible for the Prosecution to sustain. So we submit that the crime of genocide requires a special intent, an intent that has been recognised by this Court and the Courts of Rwanda, and that that special intent is necessary to elevate the crime above the other criminal offences for which this Court has jurisdiction over. In oral argument today, it was in fact conceded - and I wrote the page and line number down, it's in fact page 35, line 11 and 12 of the transcript today - it was actually conceded that the defendant would need to, and I quote "Know that he is indeed destroying a group as such." Now, coming from a background where oral argument is the norm, I certainly don't intend to tie the Prosecution to a loose word, if it be a loose word. But if that was in fact said as an accurate assertion of what the Prosecution claim the mens rea is for genocide, then with respect, it is, is it not, very, very near the dolus specialis, special intent, that the Trial Chamber applied, and a very long way indeed from the Prosecution brief which says, "The plain and ordinary meaning of Article 4 does not support the proposition that dolus specialis is required." May I move to the second limb of the Prosecutor's appeal on ground 3. Perhaps before I depart from the first, I would, if it be necessary, and I anticipate it won't, remind the Court, of course, that we have put in the 1948 convention and the Rome Statute, all of which include what we say is the special intent and its definitions. But moving to the second limb of the Prosecution's submission which is couched in these words: "In law and in fact, the Trial Chamber erred in paragraphs 88 to 98 when it said that the evidence does not establish beyond all reasonable doubt there existed a plan to destroy the Muslim group in Brcko or elsewhere within which the murders committed by Goran Jelisic would allegedly fit, and that the acts of Goran Jelisic were not the physical expression of an affirmed resolve to destroy, in whole or in part, a group as such, rather, were arbitrary acts of killing resulting from a disturbed personality." Now, the second limb of ground 3 alleges errors, and I quote, "in law and in fact." Now, the only error of law I have identified is the one addressed in the first limb of ground 3, and I for my part have not identified either, in the written or oral submission, what the error of law is, if it be any different, in the second limb. And I still am at a loss as to know whether that is intended to add to ground 1, or is there by way of surplusage. Turning to the facts, the Trial Chamber has been criticised for its conclusions of fact covering the ten paragraphs, 11 paragraphs, 88 to 98, and in particular, emphasis has been placed upon the reference to the mental state of Jelisic which medical reports later described as a personality disorder. The words of the Trial Chamber, in our submission, are worth examining. It's at paragraph 105. What the Trial Chamber said was this: "The words and attitude of Goran Jelisic as related by the witnesses essentially reveal a disturbed personality." It goes on to say that, "He was immature, narcissistic, had a hunger to fill a void, and a concern to please his superiors." In our submission, those are conclusions that the Trial Chamber was perfectly capable of coming to on the evidence they had from the witnesses who were present at the time and saw the accused acting in the way that he did in and around the town of Brcko when the offences took place. Although there is a reference there to Dr. van der Bussche's report, the Trial Chamber are referring expressly to the witnesses that caused them to come to that conclusion. They're referring, we would submit, to the witnesses called by the Prosecution. The Court may think that you don't need a distinguished psychiatrist to tell you if somebody is immature. You can make that judgement yourself on the evidence that's presented to you. You don't need a psychiatrist to tell you if somebody is narcissistic or has a concern to please his superiors. These are conclusions of fact that one could make day in and day out as the trier of fact in a criminal case. There's nothing, we submit, indicative in paragraph 105 that points to the Trial Chamber, as it were, importing post-verdict reports into pre-verdict conclusions. And if I may just make a broad submission to begin with on the facts, the judgement of a Court, particularly a short written judgement following a more lengthy oral judgement, is not intended to be a complete review of each piece of evidence that has been called before the Chamber in what was inevitably a long trial. Far less is it to be a document to be examined with the same skill as a Jesuit scholar by studying an ancient Roman transcript. It is the reasoning of a Court in coming to a conclusion, a certain latitude must be allowed in their use of language which is designed only to express the conclusions that they have come to in the course of their deliberations. Obviously any judgement, certainly a written one as short as this, will inevitably fail to mention an enormous amount of the evidence that was called. It's humanly impossible to insert all the relevant evidence in a judgement of this length. It is not the intention of the Trial Chamber so to do. The error that the Prosecution make is to assume that the absence by the Trial Chamber or the failure of the Trial Chamber to allude to a particular piece of evidence indicates that they ignored it or forgot it. No such assumption can safely be made. Indeed, we would submit that the Court could confidently proceed upon the basis that the Trial Chamber was well aware of the evidence that had been presented in the most painstaking manner possible to it over month after month. It is quite wrong to say that just because a piece of evidence is not alluded to, they hadn't considered it and given it due weight. What the Trial Chamber did, in our submission, was to properly apply the law to the facts as they found them. They did it, we submit, with care, accurately applying the requirement that the law demands for the proof of the special intent necessary for the offence of genocide. The Prosecution assert that the evidence proves guilt on the offence of genocide in part because they don't accept the need for the proof of the special intent that the Trial Chamber applied to the evidence. Although in paragraph 496 at page 82, they submit in the alternative that, and I quote: "It in no way precludes his unconscious desire or a firm resolve to destroy" -- I'm sorry. I've just slightly lost my place. May I start again. The Prosecution really have two stances. First they say the Trial Chamber got it wrong because they wrongly assumed you needed a special intent or, as refined today, they did need a special intent but not what you think it means. But their second line is, "Even if we're wrong, even if the law is as we've always understood it to be and the special intent, the dolus specialis, is required, then nonetheless, the evidence here proved that special intent." I'd like to deal with that at this stage. The Prosecution -- the Trial Chamber, in our submission, correctly identified the distinction between genocide and other crimes against humanity and properly applied the facts to the law. Now, it was recognised by the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic appeal that a decision on the facts will not be reversed unless, and I quote: "The evidence relied on by the Trial Chamber could not reasonably have been accepted by a reasonable person." Page 28, paragraph 64. So do the facts provide evidence that Jelisic, with intent to destroy or in part a national, ethnic, or religious group or does he prove that he killed 12 Muslims, plus three more he admitted to that weren't the subject of charges, because they were Muslims and not as part of any wider plan? Those are the two possibilities. Either he killed the 15 people that he did, no more, for capricious reasons, narcissistic reasons, because they were Muslims, because he wanted to demonstrate the power that he had over them, or did he kill them because it was part of a scheme of ethnic cleansing and he had, when he killed those people, the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group? Those are the two questions that will decide the verdict. Could the Prosecution prove the second. Well, we invite the Court to extend its analysis of the judgement from paragraph 88 right through to paragraph 108 because in our submission, it reveals a detailed and careful analysis of the evidence. There are three possible conclusions. One is that there wasn't sufficient evidence of genocide at all; two, there was not sufficient evidence to prove genocide beyond reasonable doubt; or three, there was evidence from which the Trial Chamber could be satisfied that genocide had been proved. Each of those propositions is directed, of course, against Jelisic personally. The judgement identified many inconsistencies in the evidence as to how people were selected for execution, and indeed often there was no selection at all but it was totally random. It emphasised that the evidence proved that 66 people died in the Brcko camp - not obviously all killed by the defendant - despite Exhibits 12 and 13 that suggested a death toll of more. That had to be viewed against a total Muslim population of 22.000 in 1991, approximately 55 per cent of the total, and a remaining population of about 2.000 to 3.000 Muslims after the destruction of the bridges on the 30th of April, 1992, that coincided with calls for the town to be divided, on ethnical grounds, into three parts. The evidence quoted in the Prosecution submission is, of course, selective. The Trial Chamber had the benefit of seeing and hearing all of the witnesses. They did not accept that the evidence of the various lists referred to, of which I have alluded to two in particular but of course there were more, were evidence from which they were satisfied genocidal intent could be inferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, I don't want to cramp your style. Would you be much longer? Because we are hoping to adjourn for the day around 5.00, 5.15, and to take a break, a short break, but that must accommodate itself to your convenience at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: If the Court were to rise now for a break, I would certainly finish by 5.15. I may finish, I hope, by 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, then, the sitting stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The sitting is resumed. Mr. Clegg.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: If I could just take the Appeal Chamber to the judgement of the Trial Chamber, to firstly paragraph 65. The conclusion there: "Although the Trial Chamber is not in a position to establish the precise number of victims ascribed to Goran Jelisic in the period in the indictment, it notes that in this instance the material element of the crime of genocide has been satisfied. Consequently, the Trial Chamber must evaluate whether the intent of the accused was such that his acts must be characterised as genocide." Now, the only conclusion the Trial Chamber is coming to there is effectively that the actus reus necessary for the crime of genocide has been proved. It's not making any conclusion about whether in fact genocide has been proved as taking place in the camp where he worked. If you turn to paragraph 87, it there identifies the first question that they address. "Before even ruling on the level of intention required, the Trial Chamber must first verify whether an act of genocide has been committed as the accused cannot be found guilty of having aided and abetted in a crime of genocide unless that crime has been established." Then considers the evidence as to whether genocide has been proved, and at paragraph 98 comes to this conclusion: "The Trial Chamber considers that in this case the Prosecutor has not provided sufficient evidence allowing it to be established beyond all reasonable doubt that there existed a plan to destroy the Muslim group in Brcko or elsewhere wherein which the murders committed by the accused would allegedly fit." Now that, we submit, is a crucial finding of fact. What the Trial Chamber has there determined is that there was no sufficient proof that there was a genocidal plan put into place in Brcko at the time the appellant committed his killings. That crucial decision is far more important when one comes to consider the ultimate verdict than the second decision, namely, the one that is addressed at paragraph 99, namely, whether as a perpetrator, Jelisic could be declared guilty of genocide. Now I -- and the Trial Chamber concede that is theoretically possible, but clearly has obvious evidential difficulties. What the Trial Chamber concluded was that the events as proved in Brcko did not establish that a genocidal plan was in fact being put into operation by those working in the camp. Now, the murders that Jelisic pleaded guilty to committing, and they were the subject matter of an agreement of facts between the parties before the trial for genocide commenced, were, firstly, lacking in any degree of organisation. They lacked planning, and although there was a degree of consistent method, they were, in many senses, random. All of those factors are inconsistent with the existence of a personal genocidal plan that would be necessary in the light of the Trial Chamber conclusion at paragraph 98. They've rejected an overall plan in which he played a part and are now seeking to say whether, in effect, he was on a one-man genocide mission, and have come to the conclusion that the lack of planning and the random nature of his conduct could not enable Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. them to come to that conclusion, despite the fact that he chose most, if not all, of his victims because they were Muslims, and despite the fact the evidence gave propensity to be cruel to them; as did, I venture to suggest, almost every defendant before this Court has since its inception, going right back to the first case of Dusko Tadic who evinced a propensity to kill Muslims and to be cruel to them, but he wasn't guilty of genocide. Firstly, there was no plan to destroy the Muslim group in Brcko. That is a conclusion in paragraph 98. I've just read it. Secondly, there is no evidence that Jelisic alone formed such a plan, which follows in paragraphs 99 and onwards. If necessary, we would submit that when properly analysed, the evidence does not meet the bare sufficiency test in Rule 98 because in the absence of evidence of a genocidal plan embracing all of the killings, there was, in truth, nothing to suggest that he was on an individual genocidal mission. Indeed, his actions identified by the Trial Chamber in allowing people to be released, often on a whim, often at random, is inconsistent with there being a genocidal plan. And there can be no doubt that hundreds and hundreds of Muslims were released from this camp, and true, some were later rearrested; and true, some did disappear; and true, some, very sensibly, fled, but the fact of the matter is that hundreds and hundreds, if not thousands, were actually released alive. And it is, with respect, no surprise that the Trial Chamber came to the conclusion that the very charging of genocide in this -- on the facts of this particular case was, frankly, overcharging or overindicting a case where there had, in truth, been a complete admission by the accused to every killing that he had been responsible for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, I sense an assumption underlying your submissions to the effect that proof of the existence of a plan is a legal ingredient of the crime of genocide. Now, it may be that there is some disputation on this matter. Am I right in saying that the Prosecution -- in my impression, that the Prosecution has put this matter in issue and are you proposing to reply to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I don't submit that there must -- that it is a legal requirement that there is a plan of genocide embracing more than one person. As an evidential matter, it is difficult to envisage a case of genocide without there being evidence of such a plan, but it isn't a legal ingredient of the offence. It's possible for one person to commit genocide all by himself, in theory, as the Trial Chamber recognised. Again, in practice, it would be very difficult to imagine such a case. But it could occur and, in a sense, that would negate the necessity for a plan unless you could, as it were, create your own plan, put it into operation all by yourself, which would be no more than acting on the basis of your own special intent which you'd formed. So I'm not suggesting it was a legal requirement, but it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I fully understand your position on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It is, we submit, a matter of evidence that will almost invariably be required before the offence can be proved. Now, we say the Prosecution brief contains serious errors of understanding of the Trial Chamber's reasoning. What the Prosecution brief asserts at paragraph 494, at page 81, is and I quote: "The Trial Chamber finding that the accused `individual perpetrator' did not act with genocidal intent is based exclusively on the conclusion that he killed arbitrarily rather than with the clear intention to destroy a group." With respect, that does no justice to the reasoning of the Trial Chamber at all. They expressly referred to his conduct in setting Muslims free and made specific reference in a footnote to Witness E, who gave evidence about that. It concluded the killings were opportunistic and that his behaviour was inconsistent. Inconsistent, opportunist, and random behaviour legitimately can be weighed against the contention that he had formed a special intent to act in a personally genocidal way towards the Muslim community, but it is quite wrong to assert, as they do, that that was the exclusive basis for the Trial Chamber's conclusion. All consideration of his personal state of mind has to be looked at against the far more important conclusion that the existence of a plan to destroy the Muslim group in Brcko had not been proved. Can I just say a word about the approach that has been adopted by the Prosecutor in part where it says to the Appeals Chamber, the people in Brcko regard this as genocide. You must, as it were, so describe it to give justice to the deceased and the survivors. If -- and I assume that there is some evidential basis for them saying that, if it be true, the distinction between the crime, a war crime, and genocide is obviously a specific legal distinction. Bluntly, it matters not what a member of the public might think about a description being applied to the individual crimes. It does nothing to assist the Appeals Chamber, as it were, to pray in aid the impact of any decision on the survivors or the public at large if they cannot prove, and they cannot prove, an essential ingredient of the crime of genocide, then no genocide is proved. It still means that Jelisic will remain convicted of serious crimes against humanity for which he will obviously pay an appropriate penalty. Nobody quarrels with that. It's not as though this Court were excusing his conduct in some way by not giving it the legal description of genocide. The relief sought by the Prosecution, finally, is a retrial. For reasons I've already said, if ground 1 and ground 2 either succeed or fail, we would say there should be no retrial unless the Prosecution are right on ground 3, because if they're not right on ground 3, the Trial Chamber came to the right conclusion, even if it was by the wrong route. Even if the Prosecution were right, even if they were, and there was some prima facie evidence of genocide, we would submit that the decision to order a retrial is discretionary. And where somebody has spent three years in custody already, he is still only a young man, and where all of the witnesses have already undergone the painful ordeal of having to relive these events once by giving evidence, the Court is entitled to reflect, in light of the guilty pleas that he has already tendered, where the interests of justice do in fact demand that there be a retrial in this case. And the Appeal Chamber would be perfectly entitled to bear in mind the pragmatic factors, including, firstly, when a retrial could realistically take place in the light of the backlog that exists in this Chamber; and secondly, whether in the light of the pressure that exists on Court time, a retrial would in any event be justified. Those submissions are, of course, only made on the basis that the Court may reject my primary submission. But I'm glad to say the break resulted in a certain concentration of my mind within my allotted time. That concludes my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have one question with two parts, Mr. Clegg. I have a little difficulty reconciling what I think I heard you say that as to the proper standard of review on 98 bis -- or I'm sorry, the proper standard that the Trial Chamber should have applied, that of whether any reasonable Trial Chamber could find that the Prosecution had made its case beyond a reasonable doubt, a so-called objective standard, as it were, with what I believe you said later on, and that is that we should consider it that the Trial Chamber applied the correct law to the facts as they found them, and then you cited to us a passage from Tadic dealing with discretion of the Appellant Court normally not to overrule a trial court's finding unless it was grossly in error. Now, I think you can anticipate my question. How do you apply an objective standard of what any reasonable Trial Chamber would do if you have already decided that this Trial Chamber is entitled to deference on certain basic findings of fact, unless, of course, the facts were stipulated or something like that? It seems as though you're combining an objective standard, but then saying it can only be applied to facts which we must give discretion to this Trial Chamber's finding. Might not a different reasonable Trial Chamber have made different findings of fact which might perhaps have led it to a different conclusion on the standard?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes. I think I expressed myself badly. The test that I submit should be applied at the Rule 98 stage is whether a, whether a reasonable Trial Chamber properly applying the facts to the law could safely return a verdict. We say that that should be the test at that stage. And that is personal to -- that must be looked at, as it were, through the eyes or mind of the Trial Chamber concerned, so -- I'm not expressing myself very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It's a very difficult concept, I'm well aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: The Rule 98 ought to be an objective test. I think I must concede that. In other words, could a reasonable Trial Chamber convict on this evidence? It could reasonably; therefore, absent anything else, the trial were to continue. The test that the Appellant Court applies is in many ways the same test but differently described. You look at the decision of the Trial Chamber on the facts and say, well, could a reasonable Trial Chamber have come to the conclusion that he was guilty or not guilty of that charge? Even though you yourself sitting in your appellant capacity might think if I had been trying it, I probably would have found him guilty or I'd probably have found him not guilty. If a reasonable judge could have come to the opposite conclusion, you don't disturb the verdict. You only disturb the verdict if your conclusion is that no reasonable judge could have come to that concussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: To just follow through, I find that a little difficult to follow in the sense that if on a motion for judgement of acquittal in mid-trial you are really applying a standard that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have said, "Let's go ahead with the trial, I think there's enough evidence to make the Defence present its case," why wouldn't the proper stance for an Appellant Court be to say, "We will look at all the evidence that's in the record as at that time, and we will decide a l'insuffisance or sufficiency whether any reasonable Chamber could have decided that there was in fact enough evidence to proceed with the trial rather than giving the usual kind of deference we give to the judgement at the end of all of the evidence. I guess that's my basic question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I think the answer to that is because you're a Court of Appeal, not a court of review. You're not reviewing what the Trial Chamber has decided in a strict way; in other words, you're looking at what they've done, seeing if they've come to the right conclusion. What you're doing is considering an appeal that they couldn't have come to that conclusion. So it's a difference or a distinction between the sort of function that you would have if you were to undergo a retrial here of the facts as opposed to sitting in an appellant capacity to see if something has gone procedurally wrong in the lower court, or a decision has been made that no reasonable Tribunal could have arrived at. Now, there are quite powerful reasons why that ought to be the case. The first is, of course, that none of this -- no one in this court has seen the witnesses and have been able to form that essential judgement that a Trial Chamber can form through actually seeing and judging a witness when they give evidence. There's no point just reading out what a witness says from a cold transcript. Everybody in court might have said, "Well, he might say that, but I don't believe a word he said." So you haven't got the advantage of having seen the evidence, and in a system of criminal justice is dependent on primarily oral testimony, the reliance on oral testimony that is the root to the verdict for the Trial Chamber, and that's why I would submit the test is as I've adumbrated it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just if I may, a follow-up on the questions asked by my colleague, is there any merit in the view that the Tadic test to which you have referred pertains to the final evaluation made by the Trial Chamber of all the evidence in the case, and more particularly, at the stage where it is making a definitive finding of guilt or innocence? At that stage, would it be possible to say that the Appeals Chamber could be asked to reevaluate the questions of credibility and weight; whereas here you have a situation in which, normally speaking, judgement stands suspended on questions of credibility, weight, and reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I wouldn't, with respect, accept any distinction of the type that you've postulated. The issues of credit, weight, and reliability must primarily be formed on the assessment of the witness who gave the evidence. It's not frequent that another witness will be able to affect the weight or reliability unless the witness gives some evidence that is contrary to the first. So that the primary assessment of the witness must be based on what view the Court formed of the witness as he or she gave evidence. There ought not to be a different test performed by the Appellate Chamber or a different standard applied to the Appellate Chamber from the Tadic test merely because the finding here was made at the close of the case for the Prosecution, one reason being supposing the Court had said, as I gave by way of example, "It may help you to know, Mr. Greaves, that we are most unimpressed with the quality of evidence that has been called so far," and Mr. Greaves was astute enough to spot a broad hint when he was given it, and said, "Well, I think in those circumstances, I'll send my 60 witnesses back from where they came. I'll call no evidence." Then you would, presumably have to apply the Tadic test because it would be a test based on all the evidence. Here, in reality, one's in the same position. The Court -- and one can see that the normal courtesies that normally exist between bar and bench did slightly collapse in this case towards the end and that may be reflective of some of the problems that occurred, but had the Court done that, no complaint could be made. The fact that they didn't shouldn't alter the standard that's applied by this Chamber because it is, nonetheless, a decision made on all the evidence that they heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last question. This has to do with the question of intent. Now, the Statute itself tells us what kind of intent is contemplated, intent to destroy in whole or in part a national group, et cetera, but is there a preliminary question as to what "intent" itself means? This morning, Mr. Bergsmo gave us an analytical framework in which he spoke of a volitional act, a cognitive act, and I think he mentioned the word "desire." The question is this: Does intent there mean a purely or a merely volitional act or does it means a volitional act plus something more which makes it into a desire? I understand you to be saying, "Well, look, it's a problem of interpretation really. When the Trial Chamber spoke of a dolus specialis, it was referring to intent in the way meant by the Prosecution, so there is no problem there."

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Certainly in the way that the Prosecution presented their oral argument today as I followed it, I agree. I think in their written brief they were adopting a rather different stance, as I attempted to identify. The word "intent" when arrived to genocide, in our submission, reflects a state of mind that the accused must have. I don't -- I'm not attracted to the words "desire" or "motive." What the Statute demands is that the person must have a state of mind, and that state of mind must be proved by the Prosecution, and that state of mind is that his actions in killing will be part of the process of, in whole or in part, destroying and so on. So he has to be killing with that state of mind as furtherance of that state of mind that he personally holds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. Clegg. We thank you very much. Mr. Prosecutor. Your short reply will be welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll be very brief on grounds 1 and 2. On ground 1, the only thing that the Prosecution wishes to say is that this invitation of my learned friend to adopt a right decision/wrong route approach in relation to the violation of the Prosecution's right to be heard is a very slippery slope, and we would request the Appeals chamber to refrain to adopt such a route in the case of a violation of fundamental rights of either party. If we had a situation in which the Prosecution, after presenting opening arguments, was deprived of its rights of calling evidence on the basis that that Trial Chamber was not persuaded of the quality of the Prosecution's case, we wouldn't be even questioning whether the final decision was correct or not. We would say that the Prosecution's right to present a case, which has been recognised by this Appellate Court, was fundamentally violated and we invite you to make a similar finding in the case of our right to be heard. As far as the second ground of appeal is concerned, at the outset, counsel for the Prosecution wishes to apologise to the Appeals Chamber for not bringing to the Appeals Chamber's attention the clear findings of the Appeals Chamber in the Celebici decision as far as the standard under Rule 98 bis is concerned, which is incorporated in paragraph 434 of the decision, and it adopts precisely the same standard that the Prosecution is advocating for. Two points of clarification, the first one dealing with Judge Wald's question this morning, picked up by my learned friend today as to whether it makes any difference when we have a single Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. judge. My learned friend is correct. We are relying on a case of the Court of Appeal of Ontario dealing with a jury case. However, that case relies on two identical decisions in the cases of single judges, and the standard that they adopt, as they say, is that it in very simple cases where the Court of Appeal is in a position to, without speculation, assess what would have happened had the case continued, that the Court of Appeal may apply a no-substantial-wrong doctrine, but in all other cases where the Court of Appeal has to engage in a speculative exercise, the Court of Appeal should refrain from doing so and that is the standard that we are advocating for. Finally, we think that basically there are sound reasons for keeping this strict division between trier of fact and trier of law regardless of the fact that it's the same Trial Chamber, and I think that Judge Wald's question highlighted the issue about this confusion between an objective standard under Rule 98 bis and deference to the Trial Chamber's discretion as a trier of fact. This shows the negative consequences of mingling both functions, and at the end of the day, the issue before you is whether at that stage of the proceedings the objective standard under Rule 98 bis was met or not. You don't have to weigh the evidence, you don't have to reassess the evidence, you just have to analyse whether that objective standard at that stage of the proceedings had been met or not. And if the answer is it had been met, then there was a clear error of law by the Trial Chamber that you have, herein, the authority to correct. That finishes our reply to grounds 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Your Honours, a few observations on the requisite mental state under Article 4. First, the Prosecution has made no concession that there is a dolus specialis or conscious desire requirement under Article 4 of the Statute. The position of the Prosecution remains as described in paragraph 4.9 of the Prosecution's brief, as elaborated by the oral submissions made this morning. The reference I made this morning to the requirement of knowledge of actual destruction of the group as such, as referred to by my learned colleague from the Defence, only refers to category (b) in paragraph 4.9 in our brief, nothing else. Category (a) in that same paragraph of course stands on its own feet, requiring conscious desire. Second, the Defence describes paragraph 66 in the Trial Chamber's judgement as a textbook definition of specific intent. It requires, according to the last sentence of that paragraph, a genocidal plan as one of two elements which it in some unusual way deduces from the particular intent element. Counsel has just conceded that there might not be an element in Article 4 of the Statute requiring a genocidal plan. The Preparatory Commission for an International Criminal Court had to deal with this question in connection with the development of the document on elements of crimes in the context of its Article 6 on genocide, and it took a different approach than that of requiring a plan of genocide. Instead, it created, it made a new element - and this was openly attested to by the delegates who took part in the negotiations - an objective contextual element to genocide which requires that the genocidal conduct, and I quote, "took place in the context of a manifest pattern of similar conduct directed against that group," or that the genocidal conduct, quote, "could itself effect such destruction." I happened to be the Tribunal's representative to these particular negotiations in New York, and it may interest the Chamber that several delegates, during the negotiations, referred specifically to the “Jelisic scenario” when this element was being discussed. The fact that the language says "a manifest pattern of similar conduct," and does not say "a manifest pattern of other genocidal acts," or "an objectively existing genocide," is a reflection of the desire of delegates to ensure that the situation where you have a campaign of persecution out of which arises one or more perpetrators who have the necessary genocidal intent must not fall outside the scope of the Genocide Convention, and it was in that connection that delegates, lawyer delegates, especially from Canada, would refer to the Jelisic scenario as an important case that had to be kept within the scope of application of Article 6 of the ICC Statute. Interestingly, the Commission had the courage to change the law as it is spelled out in the Genocide Convention insofar as the objective context of genocide is concerned, but they did nothing of the sort when it comes to the mental state requirement. Instead, if anything, they toned down the language of the mental state requirement. Whereas in the Statute it says "with intent to destroy," et cetera, it now says in the ICC elements document that, the accused must simply have intended to destroy in whole or in part that group as such. And, Your Honours, the word "intended" in this particular context has been used in 12 of the offences in Article 8 of the ICC Statute, which deals with war crimes. Your Honours, are all those offences dolus specialis or conscious desire offences? We humbly submit that that is not the case. Three, the Defence suggests that the only difference between crimes against humanity and genocide is the specific intent requirement for genocide. But what about the elements for crimes against humanity requiring, first, the existence of a widespread or systematic attack; secondly, that the conduct of the accused was part of such a widespread and systematic attack; thirdly, that the accused knew that his conduct was part of such a widespread or systematic attack; and fourthly, which is specific to the Statute of the Tribunal, the requirement that there was an armed conflict? None of those four elements apply to the crime of genocide. Four, the Defence seems to attempt to reawaken the old discussion on rulers of state and genocide, suggesting, effectively, that only the authors of genocide can be held liable for genocide. This view was advanced by France during the negotiations of the genocide convention. I refer to the proposal A/C.6/224 which we have provided, we have provided transcripts of the discussions on that proposal to the Chamber. The discussions were concluded with a vote. Forty states were against the proposal, two states voted in favour. The Chamber should not accept a view which, if it was applied to Nazi Germany, would convict one commander of a death camp for genocide, whereas another commander of another camp could merely be described as having been militarily ambitious with fundamentally different verdicts and sentences. Five, the Defence refers to ad hoc Tribunal jurisprudence. The Jelisic judgement is, of course, the only ICTY judgement on genocide so far which is why this appeal is so important and why it is so important that the legal questions concerning genocide be properly briefed. One of the first, if not the first, of the ICTR decisions on genocide was Akayesu. The Prosecution is of course aware that this judgement refers to special intent or dolus specialis, but at the same time in paragraph 520, it refers to "knew or should have known" as the requisite standard. This is a standard that is lower than both categories (b) and (c) in paragraph 4.9 of the Prosecution's submission. "Should have known" is not even a probability standard, one could argue. The Prosecution submits that this seeming contradiction in the Akayesu judgement is such that the judgement cannot be used against the Prosecution position set out in section 4(B) of our brief. The later Rutaganda and Musema judgements express agreement with the Akayesu finding on genocidal intent and, as such, they remain tainted by that same contradiction. In any event, none of these decisions are binding on this Appeals Chamber. Six, the Prosecution does not share the understanding of Defence of the texts submitted written by Gil Gil. And finally, the Prosecution position remains that one need not resort to supplementary means of interpretation to conclude that dolus specialis is not the only mental state that satisfies Article 4. This position follows from the wording of the mental state in Article 4, read in its context and in light of the object and purpose of Article 4 and the Genocide Convention. I then pass the word to my learned colleague, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can be very brief, I think. The question of law contained within our ground of appeal for which my learned friend Mr. Clegg was searching is fully argued at 4.89 and following in our brief, and is an argument that didn't need repeating in the limited time today, and it's to the effect that motive cannot -- or can affect legal intent. That was the legal argument. It's been fully argued in writing before you. Second, one word about judgements, whether they are full or not. Frequently in this Tribunal they are indeed full. When they are not full, and when they have not followed argument, it is less and less possible to place reliance on them. The suggestion, and I simply stand by our earlier position, that they correctly applied the law to the facts is countered by the mass of material which I have only, of course, been able to summarise which shows not only evidence totally overlooked, and I drew your attention to a couple of examples, but points manifestly to contrary arguments that would have been stimulated by consideration of the evidence and which simply were never reflected in the judgement and, by inference, in the argument. It is not the case, that is, it is accepted that Jelisic killed only 15 people. Those he admitted for the other crimes for which he was sentenced, yes; but the genocide evidence at trial showed direct and other responsibility for many more, which is one of the reasons why short-circuiting that trial was such a wrong for the Trial Chamber to have done. Likewise, the figure of 66 killed is not an accepted figure at all. The Chamber will know from our pleadings that there are several pieces of evidence pointing to 2.000 of the 3.000 remaining Muslims being killed, and of course, the evidence we've had of the target group that was selected. It is not the case that the schedule before you is selective. On the contrary, it was produced for me and under our supervision, but by someone comparatively a stranger to the case. And it is because we knew of the problems that come with assessing evidence of this scale, not particularly large trial, but a substantial trial, and because of the way the defendant answered questions, moving the agenda himself, we simply identified topics and had them selected. I accept my learned friend Mr. Clegg's analysis of how the Chamber was moving between paragraph 65 and 87. I accept his analysis of what the Chamber were doing. I entirely reject as remotely sustainable on the available evidence the Chamber's finding that there was no plan. This was not -- and again, I can simply ask Your Honours to look at the material with more time and reflection, random to a degree but well within an overarching plan that wasn't just binding on Jelisic, but was, as he himself complained, being put into effect by others who were as guilty as he. Not a question of hundreds and hundreds released, very much more guarded than that. And as to the particular actions of Jelisic, I dealt in closed session with a topic on that this morning. And as we may discover tomorrow, the Prosecution's position, as reflected not least by the officer dealing with him in his interviews, was that his responses at the time, as indeed in an interview, were cynical and self-serving; although the Chamber will probably have in mind the quotation from the case of Pole that I think finds expression in one of our pleadings to the effect -- this is from, of course, the war crimes at Nuremberg trials. "It is not an unusual phenomenon in life to find an isolated good deed emerging from an evil man." The quote goes on, "Because of convenience, caprice, or even a sudden ephemeral gleam of benevolence forcing its way through a callused heart, even a murderer can help a child to safety. A grim humour can cause a slayer to save his intended victim, but whatever the cause which motivated "X's" benevolence to `Y,' a kind deed is not enough to obliterate his indifference to the wholesale suffering of which he could not but be aware, and to alleviate which, in spite of his protestations, he did little or nothing." So though we do not accept and did not accept any good motivations by Jelisic, for we said the matters referred to by my learned friend are explicable otherwise, even if there were such isolated acts of no significance, the suggestion that the ordinary person can make findings about narcissistic behaviour and so on is simply, and with great respect, wrong. The terminology in that paragraph is all borrowed effectively from the last report, I think, of van den Bussche submitted to the Chamber after they had made their decision about genocide. I only return to the reference to Brcko and its inhabitants to correct a misapprehension of my learned friend. Of course, civilian residents of a community have no right to have a word that they use in one way determine in the way they'd like to have it used by a Court. Of course not. And as I said, their only interest was in having the matter fully determined. And since your discretion is prayed in aid by reference to the victims' witnesses, if I didn't say this this morning, our understanding is, and we make our application for a retrial on this basis, that the witnesses are indeed willing to give evidence, many of them being far more concerned that the matter should be fully litigated, even at their own inconvenience. Those are all our conclusions -- our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you one question. Mr. Clegg, as I understand him, argued this: You devoted some attention this morning to demonstrating that there was evidence on which a reasonable tribunal of fact could bring if a verdict of guilty. I understood him to be saying that that isn't the point. That you had to show that there was no evidence on which the Tribunal in this case could find as it did. It isn't therefore a question of whether there was any evidence on which a reasonable tribunal of fact could find otherwise; it's a question as to whether there was any evidence on which this Tribunal could find as it did. Would an answer be this, would there be any merit in an answer like this, that the issue here is really different from the issue which arises on the final decision in evidence. This is a mid-trial decision, and the question is whether the Prosecution evidence, if accepted, could sustain the conviction by a reasonable tribunal of fact, and that entitles you to point to evidence which had that effect, evidence which would have entitled a reasonable tribunal of fact to decide that the evidence before it could sustain a conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's a formulation with which I know we all entirely agree, for the reasons advanced by my learned friend Mr. Guariglia and for other reasons. And I would respectfully dissent from the view my learned friend Mr. Clegg has expressed about how judges in fact deal with cases midway. As I think Your Honour suggested, it's not just a question of technically suspending judgement as a judge until termination of the case, evidence, and argument. It is, if you are to do the job of -- if one is to do the job of judge properly, genuinely to suspend judgement until all the evidence is in and all the argument is advanced. It is for that reason that I touched on the issue in response to the observation by Her Honour Judge Wald earlier about the conduct of judges trying cases alone. And if I may respectfully trespass on your time for this single point. In adopting Your Honour's formulation, what would be appropriate for a single judge is to be applied even more so to a bench of three judges. Mr. Clegg says, "Well, effectively, the single judge could at the end of a non-criminal case, civil personal injury action, could say to counsel, well, I'm not very impressed by your specialist doctor." He could. It's a dangerous course to take because he might infect the conduct of the trial in a way he can't predict, but he might do it, dangerous, slippery slope though it may be. But where there are three judges with three brains and three minds, it would be quite wrong even to attempt such provisional formulations of views because they must genuinely, in our respectful submission, genuinely suspend judgement, and that reinforces the proposition that Your Honour made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If I could ask one last question following that group. Is it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to Judge Wald, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What is your position on Mr. Clegg's view that an Appellant Chamber looking at a Trial Chamber who has in fact -- let's say they applied the proper standard. Let's say the standard -- they applied the objective standard down below and came to the conclusion that an acquittal was necessary. When the Appellant Chamber goes to look at what they did, is that a question of law to which no deference should be given to the Trial Chamber, or is it some kind of mixture and some kind of deference ought to be given to the Trial Chamber? I know the situation in my own country: It would be a question of law and sufficiency of the evidence, but I'm interested in your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm quite satisfied in this Tribunal, as I suspect in most if not all, it is a pure question of law and it is an objective test. There's something that I was going to add to that. Let me just think if I can retrieve it. I know what I was going to add. It's pretty hard actually to see how the matter could ever truly come to light save in these exceptional circumstances where the Trial Chamber's gone wrong and accelerated its own decision, because putting on one side the truly marginal cases which don't apply here, the sort of case that perhaps Mr. Clegg pointed out, the completely destroyed witness, the marginal identification case, put those on one side, any Chamber seeing evidence of - forget genocide - robbery and evidence going to show that the defendant was the robber, two composite elements required for the crime, any Chamber would have to say, "Well, there's evidence that could go forward." Any Appeals Chamber would have to say the same thing. And for the Trial Chamber to have formed a capricious or even a genuine provisional view on the validity of the identifying evidence would be wrong. They have to bide their time. So it's always going to be difficult to postulate examples where this would come to light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance, Mr. Nice. I take it that there ends the hearing on this particular appeal by the Prosecution. Tomorrow we will take Mr. Clegg's appeal at 9.30, following the same sequence, I believe. So now we will take the adjournment until that time.
